title: The Voice on Patmos
sum: John is in exile on Patmos, a small island off the coast of modern Turkey, "because of the word of God." On "the Lord's day" he hears a voice like a trumpet. He turns and sees Jesus, shining, with hair white as wool, eyes like fire, and a sharp sword coming out of his mouth. Jesus holds seven stars and walks among seven gold lampstands, and he explains the picture himself: the stars are angels of the seven churches, and the lampstands are the churches.

The first verse tells you how to read everything that follows. God "made it known," and the KJV's "signified" may hint that he showed it in signs (see the note on 1:1). Either way, expect pictures that stand for things.

readings: Read literally

Jesus really appeared to John, and John wrote down what he saw. Many literal readers use 1:19 as the book's outline: what John has seen (chapter 1), what is now (chapters 2–3), and what will come later (chapters 4–22).
Read as symbol

The portrait is built from Daniel 7 and Daniel 10, not meant as a physical description. White hair recalls the "Ancient of Days," God himself. The sword from his mouth is his word (Isaiah 49:2; Hebrews 4:12). Jesus walking among the lampstands means he is present with his churches.

views.P: Written before AD 70. "Soon" means soon for the first readers. The "coming with the clouds" (1:7) is Christ's judgment on Jerusalem.
views.H: The book is a map of church history, from John's day to the return of Christ.
views.F: Chapters 1–3 are John's day. Most of what follows is still in the future.
views.I: The vision shows what is always true: Christ is present with his suffering people in every age.

deep.b:
The risen Jesus, piece by piece

What John seesSourceWhat it says about him
"One like a son of man" (1:13)Daniel 7:13The human figure given everlasting rule
A long robe and a gold sash (1:13)Exodus 28:4; Daniel 10:5A priest, standing among the lampstands as the priest tended the temple lamps
Hair white as wool and snow (1:14)Daniel 7:9In Daniel this is God himself, the Ancient of Days
Eyes like flames of fire (1:14)Daniel 10:6He sees everything (2:18, 23)
Feet like polished bronze, fired in a furnace (1:15)Daniel 10:6; Ezekiel 1:7Strength that cannot be shaken
A voice like the sound of many waters (1:15)Ezekiel 43:2The sound of God’s own glory
A sharp two-edged sword from his mouth (1:16)Isaiah 11:4; Isaiah 49:2He judges and wins by his word (19:15)
A face like the sun (1:16)Judges 5:31; Matthew 17:2The glory seen at the Transfiguration
Seven stars in his right hand (1:16, 20)—The churches’ angels are in his grip

John takes features that Daniel gives to God and to the son of man and puts them on one figure. Without saying "Jesus is God," the picture says it.

"From the One who is"

In 1:4 John writes apo ho ōn, "from He-who-is," keeping God's name in the form used for the subject of a sentence even though Greek grammar requires another form after "from." It looks like a schoolboy's mistake, and John does break Greek grammar often (1:5 has "the faithful witness" in the same wrong case; see also 2:13, 2:20 and 4:8). But his breaks come in patterns, many follow Hebrew ways of speaking or mark Old Testament allusions, and many scholars (R. H. Charles, Aune) think they are often on purpose. Here most think he refused to change God's name, which comes from Exodus 3:14 in the Greek Old Testament: "I am ho ōn, the One who is." The phrase "who is, who was and who is to come" adds a twist: we expect "who will be," but God is the one who comes.

The road the letters traveled

LegRough distanceNotes
Patmos to EphesusAbout 60 miles by seaEphesus, the province’s leading city and port, comes first
Ephesus to SmyrnaAbout 35 miles northAlong the coast road
Smyrna to PergamumAbout 65 miles northThe old royal capital
Pergamum to ThyatiraAbout 40 miles southeastThe road turns inland
Thyatira to SardisAbout 35 miles southAlong the Hermus valley
Sardis to PhiladelphiaAbout 30 miles southeastOn the imperial post road
Philadelphia to LaodiceaAbout 45 miles southeastThe circuit ends in the Lycus valley

The seven cities are listed in the order a messenger would reach them on a loop of Roman roads, a point first made by William Ramsay (1904). Distances are approximate.

Patmos was a small, rocky island that Rome used as a place of banishment. The Monastery of Saint John, founded in 1088, still stands there, and visitors are shown the "Cave of the Apocalypse" as the place of the vision.

Revelation belongs to a family of Jewish "apocalypses" written between about 200 BC and AD 100, such as 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch. They share visions, angel guides, symbolic beasts, numbered periods of time, and a final judgment. Revelation is unusual because its author uses his own name; most apocalypses claim to be by ancient heroes like Enoch.

echoes: Daniel 7:9–14; Daniel 10:5–6; Zechariah 12:10; Exodus 19:6; Isaiah 44:6

settings.what: The title and the first blessing
settings.by: John
settings.to: the one who reads the book aloud in the churches, and those who hear it
settings.when: at the very start, before the letter's greeting
settings.why: The book calls itself an unveiling given "to show his slaves what must happen soon." Its first blessing is for the reader and the listeners in a gathered church, so the book was made to be heard together, not studied alone. It is the first of seven blessings in Revelation (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14), each a word spoken straight to the hearers.

settings.what: The letter's greeting and opening praise
settings.by: John
settings.to: the seven churches in the province of Asia, gathered to hear the book read aloud
settings.when: at the start, in the form of a letter like Paul's
settings.why: Revelation begins as a real letter, so everything after it is addressed to these churches. The greeting names God "the one who is, who was, and who is coming," and calls Jesus "the ruler of the kings of the earth": a bold title in cities where the emperor was hailed as lord. The praise reminds small and pressured groups that they are already "a kingdom and priests."

settings.what: John's call on Patmos
settings.by: John, describing the risen Jesus who speaks to him
settings.to: the seven churches, who share "the suffering, the kingdom, and the endurance" with John
settings.when: on the Lord's day, while John was on Patmos, most think as an exile
settings.why: The vision shows Jesus walking among the seven lampstands, the churches. Before any warning, the readers learn that he is present with them and holds their "angels" in his hand. His words "Don't be afraid" are for John and also for churches that feared prison and death. Each letter that follows begins with a piece of this picture.

traditions.q: John was in the Spirit "on the Lord's day" (1:10). Does that mean Sunday, and should Christians keep Sunday instead of the Sabbath?
views: Yes. The Lord's day is Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and from the start Christians gathered on it (the Didache calls it the Lord's own day). Sunday fulfills the Sabbath and takes its place as the day to worship and rest (Catechism 2174–2175).

Yes. Sunday, the day of the resurrection, is the Lord's day and the "eighth day" of the new creation, kept with the Divine Liturgy. Saturday is still honored as the Sabbath of creation: Orthodox canons forbid strict fasting on both days, and Saturday is the day the dead are remembered.

It means Sunday, but Sunday is not a law. The Augsburg Confession (article 28) says the Sabbath of Moses has ended and the church chose the Lord's day in Christian freedom, as a good order for worship, not as a command that binds the conscience.

It means Sunday, and the Sabbath command still applies to it. The Westminster Confession calls the first day "the Lord's day," citing this verse, and says it is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy until the end of the world.

It means Sunday. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 8) calls the first day "the Lord's Day," a Christian institution for regular worship and rest that commemorates the resurrection; Baptists differ on how strictly its rest should be kept.

No. The only day the Bible says the Lord owns is the seventh day, of which Jesus said he is Lord (Mark 2:28), and nothing here says Sunday. Adventists keep the Saturday Sabbath and teach that Sunday worship came in later, mainly through the church at Rome.

title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum and Thyatira
sum: Jesus dictates a letter to each of seven real churches in what is now western Turkey. Every letter has the same parts: a title of Jesus (most of them taken from the vision in chapter 1), "I know what you do," praise or warning, "Whoever has an ear should listen," and a promise "to the one who wins the victory."

Ephesus works hard and tests false teachers, but has lost its first love. Smyrna is poor and persecuted and gets no correction at all. Pergamum lives "where Satan's throne is," stays loyal, but tolerates compromise. Thyatira is growing in love and service, but tolerates a false prophet called "Jezebel."

The Thyatira letter is full of sexual words: "sexual sin," "adultery," a bed, and a woman nicknamed Jezebel. Below the four views is a closer look at what those words mean, why the Bible so often describes false worship as prostitution, what was happening in Thyatira, and how different readers have understood her.

Three times in this chapter Jesus quotes a claim and answers it: false "apostles" at Ephesus, those "who say they are Jews and are not" at Smyrna, and Jezebel at Thyatira, "who calls herself a prophet." The topic page <button class="linkish" data-go="tp-say-are-not">"Those who say they are... and are not"</button> explains the pattern, who these people were, and why claims to a name, like Roman citizenship, carried legal weight.
caption: Map drawn from the cities’ real locations. The red loop follows the letters’ order, a natural road circuit starting from the port nearest Patmos.
readings: Read literally
These were real congregations with real problems around AD 95. Archaeology confirms many local details, such as Pergamum's huge altar of Zeus and its early temple to the emperor.
Read as symbol
Seven means complete, so the seven churches stand for the whole church. Every letter ends by speaking to "the churches," plural, so every church is meant to hear all seven.

views.P: Real churches under Roman and synagogue pressure before the Jewish war.
views.H: Seven ages of church history. Ephesus is the age of the apostles, Smyrna the age of the martyrs, Pergamum the age of Constantine, Thyatira the medieval church.
views.F: Real first-century churches. Many dispensationalists also see the seven "church ages" in them.
views.I: Seven kinds of churches that exist in every generation.

deep.b:
Is Jezebel called a prostitute?

Not quite, and the difference matters. Revelation never calls her a pornē, "prostitute." That word is saved for Babylon in chapter 17. What the letter says is this:

  • She teaches Jesus's slaves and leads them astray "into sexual sin" (porneusai, 2:20). This is a verb from the same family as pornē. Its root meaning is "to sell yourself," but by John's day it covered any sex outside marriage.
  • She refuses to repent of her "sexual sin" (porneia, 2:21).
  • Those who "commit adultery with her" (moicheuontas, 2:22) will suffer. Adultery is a different word. It means breaking a marriage.
  • Her "children" will be put to death (2:23).

So the letter uses two pictures. Jezebel herself is pictured as sexually loose. The church members who follow her are pictured as cheating spouses. That second picture only works if they are already "married," and in the Bible God's people are married to God (Hosea 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 19:7). Whatever else is going on, John is describing a betrayal of Jesus by people who belong to him.

Why the Bible links sex and idols

For readers who know the Old Testament, this language was familiar. The prophets described Israel's worship of other gods as prostitution and adultery again and again:

  • The law. Making deals with the Canaanites would lead Israel to "chase after their gods like prostitutes" (Exodus 34:15–16).
  • The prophets. Hosea married an unfaithful wife as a living picture of Israel (Hosea 1–3). Jeremiah says Israel has gone after many lovers like a prostitute (Jeremiah 3:1). Ezekiel 16 and 23 are long, painful poems about Jerusalem and Samaria as unfaithful wives.
  • Baal of Peor. In Numbers 25:1–2, "the people began to commit sexual sin with the daughters of Moab," and the women invited them to the sacrifices for their gods, where "the people ate." Sex and idol food together, exactly the pair in 2:14 and 2:20. Numbers 31:16 blames this on Balaam's advice, which is why the letter to Pergamum mentions Balaam.
  • The real Jezebel. When Jehu came to overthrow her family, Jehoram asked, "Is it peace, Jehu?" and Jehu answered, "Peace? What peace is there, while your mother Jezebel keeps up her prostitution and her many sorceries?" (2 Kings 9:22). Nothing in 1 and 2 Kings says Queen Jezebel was literally a prostitute. Her "prostitution" was bringing Baal worship into Israel (1 Kings 16:31–33). The name "Jezebel" came with the prostitution label already attached, and the label meant idolatry.

The logic is covenant logic. Israel's relationship with God was like a marriage: exclusive, loving and binding. Worshiping another god was not just a wrong opinion. It was cheating.
A Thyatira guild banquet, as many scholars picture the problem: members recline on couches in a temple dining room, the meat comes from the god’s altar, and the evening is held in the god’s honor.

What was happening in Thyatira?

A city of trade guilds. Thyatira was a factory town. Inscriptions found there name more trade associations than in almost any other city in Asia Minor: wool workers, linen workers, garment makers, dyers, leather workers, tanners, potters, bakers, bronze smiths and slave dealers. Lydia, Paul's first convert in Europe, "sold purple cloth and came from the city of Thyatira" (Acts 16:14).

Guilds met for meals, and the meals honored gods. A guild was part trade union, part social club, part religious society. Each had a patron god, and members met for banquets, often in a temple dining room, eating meat from the god's sacrifices. Papyrus invitations from Egypt read like this: "Chaeremon invites you to dine at the couch of the lord Sarapis in the Sarapeum tomorrow." Thyatira's chief god was Apollo Tyrimnaios, a sun god, which may be why Jesus introduces himself here as "the Son of God... whose eyes are like a flame of fire" (2:18).

Staying out was costly. A Christian dyer or bronze smith who refused the guild banquets could lose customers, partners and standing. Jezebel's teaching probably said, in effect, "You can go. Idols are nothing. God knows your heart." Paul had faced a similar question at Corinth (1 Corinthians 8–10), and the Jerusalem council had asked gentile believers to keep away from "food sacrificed to idols" and "sexual sin" (Acts 15:29). Notice that Jesus ends the letter with "I am not putting any other burden on you" (2:24), almost the council's own words, with the same Greek word baros, "burden" or "load": "to place no heavier load on you than these necessary things" (Acts 15:28).

Who was she? Most scholars think she was a real woman, a respected prophet in the Thyatira church, whom John calls "Jezebel" the way we call a traitor "a Judas." She was clearly influential: she had "children," meaning followers, and had been given "time to repent." Two older guesses are worth knowing about:

  • "Your wife Jezebel." Some Greek manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus and many later ones, read "your wife Jezebel" (tēn gunaika sou). If the "angel" of the church is its leader, she would be the leader's wife. Most modern editions read "the woman," and the point is debated; see the variant at 2:20.
  • A local oracle. In 1892 Emil Schürer suggested she was linked to a shrine of the Sibyl Sambathe outside Thyatira. Few scholars accept this today, since the text places her inside the church ("you leave the woman Jezebel alone").

Literal, figurative, or both?

Readers have taken the sexual language in four main ways:

Mainly figurative: idolatry

"Sexual sin" is the prophets' word for unfaithfulness to God, and the real issue is the idol feasts. Revelation uses porneia this way for Babylon (14:8; 17:2; 18:3; 19:2), and "adultery" fits church members who are "married" to Christ. Held by many modern commentators (for example G. K. Beale and Craig Koester).

Literal: real sexual sin

Some groups in the early church taught that the body did not matter, so what you did with it did not matter either. The church fathers Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria connect the Nicolaitans with this kind of freedom. Revelation also uses these words literally elsewhere (9:21; 21:8; 22:15). Held by many traditional and futurist commentators (for example Robert Thomas and John Walvoord).

Both at once

Guild banquets could end in drinking and hired company, and Paul at Corinth had to deal with both idol meals and Christians visiting prostitutes (1 Corinthians 6:15–16; 10:7–8). On this view Jezebel opened a door that led to both. This is probably the most common middle position.

Mostly name-calling

Some scholars, such as Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Tina Pippin, note that ancient writers often attacked rival teachers, especially women, with sexual insults. They read Jezebel as a real prophet who disagreed with John about how much Christians could take part in city life, and they caution against assuming she was literally immoral. Others answer that John is quoting the Old Testament's own covenant language, not inventing an insult.

Something every view agrees on: the letter's first complaint is that the church left her alone (2:20). The warning is as much about a church that would not deal with a problem as about one woman.

How the four views read her

  • Preterist: a first-century woman in a real church, and a real dispute over guild feasts. Fulfilled in John's day.
  • Historicist: the seven churches also picture seven ages of church history. Thyatira, praised for "service" but tolerating Jezebel, is the medieval church; Jezebel is often read as the papacy or the corruption of the church through power and wealth.
  • Futurist: many dispensationalists read the letters both as real churches and as a preview of church history (the Scofield Reference Bible did this). Some see Jezebel's "children" growing into the great prostitute of chapter 17, an unfaithful church at the end of the age.
  • Idealist: Jezebel stands for any voice inside the church that makes peace with the gods of the culture: money, status, sex, nation. Her teaching sounds spiritual ("the deep things") and practical ("everyone does it").

A modern use not found in the text: some charismatic and Pentecostal writers speak of a "Jezebel spirit," a controlling or manipulative influence. Revelation itself speaks of a person and a teaching, not a spirit.

Other traditions: was there "temple prostitution"?

Many older Bible commentaries say that pagan temples were full of "sacred prostitutes," and that Jezebel's sin was joining in. The idea comes mainly from the Greek historian Herodotus, who claimed every Babylonian woman once had to sleep with a stranger at the temple of Ishtar (Histories 1.199), and from Strabo, who said Corinth's Aphrodite temple once had a thousand prostitutes (Geography 8.6.20). Recent historians, notably Stephanie Budin, argue that these stories are mostly rumor and stereotype about foreigners, and that there is little solid evidence for sacred prostitution anywhere in the ancient world. So it is safer not to imagine temple prostitutes in Thyatira. The well-attested problem is the guild banquet.

deep.title: Jezebel is Babylon in miniature
deep.b: Queen Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, daughter of Ethbaal, "king of the Sidonians" (1 Kings 16:31); Josephus calls him king of Tyre. Tyre was the great trading city of the Old Testament, and Isaiah called it a prostitute: "she will go back to earning her fee and sell herself to every kingdom of the world" (Isaiah 23:17). Revelation's Babylon is built largely from the songs against Tyre: "The kings of the earth committed sexual sin with her" (Revelation 18:3), and the cargo list of 18:12–13 follows Ezekiel 27. My reading: the Thyatira letter is a small, local preview of chapters 17–18. A Tyrian queen's name, a trading city, merchants' guilds, "sexual sin" that is really commerce with the gods, and "sorceries" (2 Kings 9:22, compare "by your magic all the nations were led astray," Revelation 18:23). "Come out of her, my people" (18:4) is the world-sized version of "unless they repent of her works" (2:22). If that is right, Babylon is not only something out there. It can start in a church's own dining room.

deep.title: The couch becomes a sickbed, and the queen is thrown down
deep.b: The Greek of 2:22 says only "I am throwing her onto a bed" (klinē). Translators add "sickbed" because of the sickness that follows. But klinē was also the word for the dining couch where guests reclined at a banquet, including the "couch of the lord Sarapis." Some commentators already hear the irony (see the note on 2:22), and I think it is intended: the couch where she ate the idol feast and "committed sexual sin" becomes the bed where she lies sick. There may be a second echo. The original Jezebel's story ends when Jehu shouts "Let her drop!" and she is thrown from a window (2 Kings 9:33). That second echo is my own suggestion. Jesus also "throws" his Jezebel, but onto a bed, after giving her "time to repent." The first Jezebel got no second chance; this one did.

deep.title: The two churches with no rebuke are the two fighting over "who is Israel"
deep.b: Only Smyrna and Philadelphia get no correction. They are also the only two letters that mention "those who say they are Jews and are not" (2:9; 3:9). To Philadelphia Jesus promises, "I will make them come and bow down before your feet" (3:9). That reverses Isaiah 60:14, where the nations bow at Israel's feet. My guess is that this pairing is deliberate. The churches that suffer for their claim to belong to Israel's Messiah are the ones Jesus fully affirms. Commentators note the Isaiah reversal, and that the two unrebuked churches are the two facing synagogue opposition is a commonplace in Hemer, Aune and Koester. My own addition is only the weight I give it. It matters for the Church and Israel question below, because it is one of the strongest single verses for the "one people" view, and it rarely comes up in popular debates.

echoes: Genesis 2:9; Numbers 22–25; 1 Kings 16:31; Psalm 2:8–9; Jeremiah 17:10

settings.what: The letter to Ephesus
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Ephesus
settings.when: written to the largest city of Asia, a port and a center of the cult of Artemis, with a temple to the emperors (dedicated about AD 89; if the later date of Revelation is right, that temple was new when the letter was read)
settings.why: Ephesus was proud, busy and full of religious rivals. The church there had stood firm against false apostles and the Nicolaitans for a long time, but in guarding the truth it had lost the love it had at first. Jesus warns that a church can be right and still lose its place. The promise of "the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" may answer the sacred grove and tree imagery of Artemis's temple.
views: Some read the "love you had at first" as love for Christ, others as love for one another, others as both.

settings.what: The letter to Smyrna
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Smyrna
settings.when: written to a loyal ally of Rome, among the first cities in Asia to build a temple to Rome, where Christians were poor and faced arrest
settings.why: The church in Smyrna gets only praise and comfort. It was poor, perhaps because believers would not join the guilds and festivals, and it was slandered by local opponents John calls "a synagogue of Satan." Accused Christians could be reported to Roman officials. Jesus promises that the suffering will be short ("ten days") and that the faithful will receive "the crown of life." Smyrna's own fame for its "crown" of buildings on the hill may lie behind the image. Polycarp, its bishop, was burned there about 155.
views: Many think they were members of the city's synagogue who opposed the believers, perhaps reporting them to the authorities. John, himself a Jew, denies them the name "Jews." Hemer suggests that after the Jewish tax of Domitian's time, Christians who did not belong to the synagogue were left exposed. Others (Frankfurter, Marshall) think the words come from a dispute inside the Jewish world over who keeps Israel's name, or point at Gentile Christians who claimed to be Jews.

These are harsh words in a quarrel between neighbors, written by a Jew about a local group in one city. They are not a verdict on Jewish people in general, and Christians have done great harm by reading them that way.

settings.what: The letter to Pergamum
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Pergamum
settings.when: written to the old royal capital, with a great altar of Zeus, the healing shrine of Asclepius (whose sign was a serpent) and the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Rome
settings.why: "Where Satan's throne is" fits a city so full of pagan worship and Roman power. The church had held firm when Antipas was killed, but some members followed "the teaching of Balaam," eating idol food and committing sexual sin, which likely meant joining the feasts of temples and trade groups. Jesus calls them to repent. The promise of "hidden manna" answers their hunger at feasts they had refused; the meaning of the "white stone" is one of many guesses.
views: Readers point to the altar of Zeus, the shrine of Asclepius, or the emperor's temple and the place where the Roman governor held court on his circuit. Several may be meant at once.
Hemer lists many proposals: a vote of acquittal, a token that admitted a guest to a feast, an amulet carrying a secret name, or a jewel like those of the high priest.

settings.what: The letter to Thyatira
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Thyatira
settings.when: written to a smaller city known for its many trade guilds (dyers, bronze workers, wool and leather workers), whose guardian god, Tyrimnos, was joined with Apollo, a son of Zeus
settings.why: Thyatira's church was growing in love and service, but it tolerated a woman prophet John calls "Jezebel" who taught that eating idol food was allowed. For a worker in Thyatira, guild life often included meals in honor of the guild's gods, and her teaching made taking part easy. Jesus, "the Son of God" with feet "like polished bronze," may answer the local son of Zeus and the bronze trade. The promise of authority over the nations is for those who refuse the compromise.
views: Most read the name as a label for a real prophet in the church, taken from the queen in 1 Kings who led Israel to worship Baal. A few see a group, not one woman.
Hemer and Ramsay think guild membership was close to necessary for trade in Thyatira. Harland thinks it was voluntary, and that John is taking a strict side in a debate among Christians.

traditions.q: Do the seven churches of chapters 2–3 stand for seven ages of church history?
views: Yes, in part. The Scofield Reference Bible says the letters are real messages to real churches, but also a prophetic outline of church history from the apostles to the end, with lukewarm Laodicea as the church of the last days.

Yes. Traditional Adventist teaching gives each church a period, from Ephesus in the apostles' age to Philadelphia in the revival of the 1840s and Laodicea in the time of the judgment. Adventists have often applied the warning to Laodicea to their own church.

No. They were real churches, and because there are seven, the number of completeness, together they stand for the whole church in every age. Victorinus, writing the oldest surviving Latin commentary (about 260), said that what is said to one church is said to all.

No. Each letter ends by saying what the Spirit says "to the churches," plural, so every letter speaks to every congregation in every age. Reformed scholars find nothing in the text that marks out periods of history.

title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea
sum: The last three letters. Sardis has "a name for being alive" but is dead, and is told to keep watch. Philadelphia has little strength, yet has kept Jesus's word. It receives an open door no one can shut and no correction at all. Laodicea is rich, proud, and lukewarm, and Jesus says he is going to vomit it out.
The book's most famous invitation comes at the end of its harshest letter: "Look! I am standing at the door, knocking." It is spoken to a church, not to unbelievers.

Philadelphia hears the "say they are Jews and are not" charge a second time, now with "but are lying," and Laodicea is quoted against itself: "You say, ‘I am rich.’" See the topic page <button class="linkish" data-go="tp-say-are-not">"Those who say they are... and are not"</button>.

readings: Read literally

Seven real churches. The details fit their cities closely. Sardis's fortress fell twice to surprise attacks. Philadelphia was shaken by earthquakes. Laodicea was a banking and medical center famous for black wool, exactly what 3:17–18 mocks.
Read as symbol
The letters move from a church that looks alive but is dead, to a weak church that is faithful, to a rich church that is useless. Outward strength is never the measure.

views.P: Real churches before AD 70. The "hour of testing" (3:10) is the coming Roman war and its effects across the empire.
views.H: Sardis is the Reformation church (alive in name), Philadelphia the missionary age of the 1700s–1800s, Laodicea the lukewarm modern church.
views.F: Many pre-tribulation readers take 3:10 ("I will keep you from the hour of testing") as a promise that the church will be raptured before the tribulation.
views.I: Every congregation can become a Sardis or a Laodicea, and every weak one can be a Philadelphia.

deep.b:
Three cities and their echoes

CityWhat it was known forHow the letter uses it
SardisOld royal capital of Lydia and King Croesus; a "safe" hilltop fortress yet taken by surprise twice, because no one was watching the walls (by Cyrus about 547 BC and Antiochus III in 214 BC)"Be on the watch" and "I will come like a thief" (3:2–3); "a few names in Sardis who have not dirtied their clothes" (3:4)
PhiladelphiaShaken by the great earthquake of AD 17 and by aftershocks for years; renamed "Neocaesarea" for Tiberius’s help and later "Flavia""I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will never go out of it again"; "On him I will write... my new name" (3:12)
LaodiceaBanking, a glossy black wool, and a medical school linked to an eye salve; rebuilt with its own money, refusing Rome’s help, after the AD 60 earthquake (Tacitus, Annals 14.27)"I am rich... and I need nothing" (3:17); "buy from me gold refined by fire... Buy white clothes... And buy eye salve" (3:18)

Hot, cold and lukewarm

Laodicea had no good water of its own and piped it in through a stone aqueduct; it arrived tepid and full of minerals, and the pipes are still crusted with deposits. Six miles away, Hierapolis had hot springs used for healing; ten miles away, Colossae may have had cool, fresh water, though the evidence for that is thin. Many scholars (following M. J. S. Rudwick and E. M. B. Green, 1958, and Colin Hemer) argue that "hot" and "cold" are both good, like Hierapolis's healing water and Colossae's refreshing water. Laodicea's problem was not that it was half-hearted rather than hostile; it was that it did no one any good. The traditional reading ("I would rather you were openly against me than half-committed") is still common. Craig Koester doubts the local link altogether: at a meal, drinks were served hot or chilled, and a lukewarm one was spat out, an image anyone could grasp.

"I am standing at the door, knocking"

Often used to invite unbelievers to faith, 3:20 is first spoken to a church that has left Jesus outside. The picture is of a shared meal, echoing the lover knocking in Song of Songs 5:2. William Holman Hunt's painting The Light of the World (1851–53, Keble College, Oxford; a later version is in St Paul's Cathedral, London) shows Jesus knocking at an overgrown door with no handle on the outside: it can only be opened from within.

Philadelphia had so many earthquakes that many people lived outside the city (Strabo, Geography 12.8.18). The promise "I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will never go out of it again" (3:12) offers the opposite: a home that never shakes.

echoes: Isaiah 22:22; Isaiah 60:14; Proverbs 3:12; Song of Songs 5:2; Isaiah 65:15

settings.what: The letter to Sardis
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Sardis
settings.when: written to a once great city, the capital of the old kingdom of Lydia, which twice fell because its watchmen did not keep guard
settings.why: Sardis had a name for being alive but was dead. Nothing in the letter speaks of persecution or false teaching; the church was simply at ease with its city. The warning, "Be on the watch" and "I will come like a thief," would sting in a city famous for being taken by surprise. A few have kept their clothes clean, a fitting image in a city known for its wool and dye trade.

settings.what: The letter to Philadelphia
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Philadelphia
settings.when: written to a small city often shaken by earthquakes, rebuilt with imperial money and once renamed for an emperor
settings.why: Like Smyrna, Philadelphia gets no rebuke. It had little strength and was opposed by "the synagogue of Satan," which may mean the believers had been shut out of the synagogue. The promise that these opponents will "come and bow down before your feet" turns around Isaiah 60:14, where the nations bow to Israel: a pointed claim that the promises to Israel belong to this little church too. Jesus, who holds "the key of David," gives them an open door that no one can shut. To people in a city where earthquakes drove residents out to the fields, he promises a place as a pillar in God's temple that "will never go out of it again," and a new name, as their city once took a new name from an emperor.
views: Many think they were members of the local synagogue who opposed or expelled the believers. John, himself a Jew, denies them the name. Others (Frankfurter, Marshall) read a dispute within the Jewish world over who is truly Israel, or think the words point at Gentile Christians who claimed to be Jews.
The words belong to a local quarrel in one city in the first century. They are not a judgment on Jewish people as a whole, and reading them that way has done great harm.

Futurist readers often take "keep you from the hour of testing" (3:10) as a promise of rescue before a future tribulation. Others read it as a promise of protection through trial, for this church first.

settings.what: The letter to Laodicea
settings.by: the risen Jesus, through John
settings.to: the church in Laodicea
settings.when: written to a rich banking city that rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 60 with its own money, known for black wool and, by many accounts, an eye salve, with water piped in from several miles away
settings.why: Laodicea's church shared its city's pride: "I am rich... and I need nothing." Jesus may answer with the city's own trades: buy true gold, white clothes instead of famous black wool, and salve for blind eyes. The lukewarm water may echo the city's piped water, lukewarm and hard to drink, in contrast to the hot springs of Hierapolis and the cold water of Colossae nearby. Even so, the letter ends with Jesus at the door, asking to share a meal.
views: Many read the image as useless water, not as a scale of zeal: hot water heals and cold water refreshes, but lukewarm does neither. Others read it as zeal versus indifference.

Ramsay and Hemer tie the gold, wool, salve and water to Laodicea's banks, black wool, medical school and aqueduct. Koester argues they are images any reader in the region would know, from dining and trade, and that the local links are weaker than they look.

traditions.q: "I in turn will keep you from the hour of testing" (3:10). Will the church be taken up to heaven before the great tribulation?
views: Yes. Jesus will come for his church in a secret rapture before seven years of tribulation, and 3:10 promises to keep believers out of that hour, not safe through it. After chapter 3 the word "church" does not appear again until 22:16, and John's call to "come up here" (4:1) pictures the rapture (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Pentecost).
Mostly yes. The Assemblies of God calls the rapture of the church "the blessed hope" and teaches that it is imminent, coming before the tribulation. Some Pentecostal groups hold other timings.

Divided. Many Baptists, especially in America, hold a pre-tribulation rapture, while others, like the Baptist scholar George Eldon Ladd, say Christ returns once, after the tribulation, and that "keep you from" means protecting believers through it, as in Jesus's prayer in John 17:15. The Baptist Faith and Message does not decide.

No separate rapture. Christ will return once, in glory, and before that the church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many (Catechism 675). Being "caught up" (1 Thessalonians 4:17) is the meeting with the Lord at that one coming.

No. Reformed teachers, like Lutherans and the Orthodox, see one visible return of Christ at the end. Believers are kept from God's wrath but not from suffering, which is what the faithful in Revelation endure.

title: The Throne in Heaven
sum: A door opens in heaven, and a voice says, "Come up here." John sees God's throne with a rainbow like an emerald, 24 elders on thrones, seven burning torches, a sea of glass, and four living creatures full of eyes: one like a lion, one like an ox, one with a human face, and one like an eagle. Day and night they sing, "Holy, holy, holy."
Before anything happens on earth, John is shown who is on the throne. Every later scene of disaster is meant to be read from this room.
readings: Read literally

Heaven is a real place, and John was shown God's actual throne room. Many futurists read "Come up here" (4:1) as a picture of the rapture of the church, and note that the word "church" does not appear again until 22:16.
Read as symbol

The scene borrows from Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1. The four creatures stand for all living creation: wild animals, tame animals, humans and birds. The 24 elders may be the 12 tribes plus the 12 apostles, God's one people from both covenants.

views.P: Heaven's court gathers to pass judgment on unfaithful Jerusalem.
views.H: The throne room is the starting point for the history that the seals unfold.
views.F: The elders picture the raptured church in heaven before the tribulation begins.
views.I: God rules now, whatever the world looks like. Worship is the true center of history.

deep.b:
What fills the throne room

What John seesSource in the Old Testament
A throne, and one seated on it (4:2)1 Kings 22:19; Isaiah 6:1; Ezekiel 1:26
Jasper and carnelian, a rainbow like emerald (4:3)Ezekiel 1:28 (the rainbow around the throne); Genesis 9:13–16
Twenty-four elders on thrones (4:4)The 24 divisions of priests (1 Chronicles 24:1–19); the 12 tribes and 12 apostles (21:12–14)
Lightning and thunder (4:5)Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16)
Seven lamps of fire (4:5)The temple lampstand; Zechariah 4:2, 10
A sea of glass like crystal (4:6)The floor "of blue lapis stone" under God’s feet (Exodus 24:10); Solomon’s bronze "sea" (1 Kings 7:23)
Four living creatures full of eyes (4:6–8)Ezekiel 1:5–10 and 10:12; Isaiah 6:2–3 (six wings, "Holy, holy, holy")

A throne room that answers Rome

Rome's emperors held court surrounded by advisers and received the crowns of client kings. In AD 63 King Tiridates of Armenia laid his crown at the foot of Nero's statue (Tacitus, Annals 15.29), and in 66 he knelt in Rome to receive it back from Nero himself (Suetonius, Nero 13). Domitian liked to be called "our Lord and God" (dominus et deus noster, Suetonius, Domitian 13.2). Against that background, the elders casting their crowns before God and singing "You are worthy, our Lord and God" (4:10–11) is a political statement: these titles belong to one throne only.

Early Christian art gave the four creatures to the four Gospel writers. The usual scheme, Jerome's, is Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle. Irenaeus, the first to link them (Against Heresies 3.11.8), gave the lion to John and the eagle to Mark. You can still see them carved on church doors and painted in the Book of Kells.

deep.title: The lamassu guardians
deep.note: similar images; Ezekiel likely knew them
deep.b: Assyrian palaces were guarded by huge stone lamassu: winged bulls or lions with human heads. Ezekiel saw his living creatures while exiled in Babylonia (Ezekiel 1:1), where such figures were familiar. Revelation's creatures share the mix of lion, ox, human and eagle. The difference is the point: the lamassu guard a king's door, while these creatures do nothing but worship.

deep.title: The throne room is laid out like Israel’s camp
deep.b: In the wilderness, Israel camped in four groups around the tabernacle (Numbers 2). Old Jewish tradition gives each lead tribe a banner: Judah a lion, Reuben a man, Ephraim an ox, and Dan an eagle. Those are the four faces around God's throne. A few writers have linked the banners to Ezekiel 1. My extension is this: if the living creatures echo the camp banners, then heaven's worship is pictured as Israel camped around God. "The Lion from the tribe of Judah" (5:5) is named while the lion-faced creature stands nearby. The Lamb who appears is then the Passover lamb at the center of the camp. Caution: the banner tradition is written down later than Revelation, so this is a possible echo, not proof.

echoes: Isaiah 6:1–3; Ezekiel 1:5–28; Exodus 19:16; Exodus 24:10; Daniel 7:9–10

settings.what: The call to come up
settings.by: the voice like a trumpet, the risen Jesus of 1:10–11
settings.to: John alone, on Patmos
settings.when: after the seven letters, as a door opens in heaven
settings.why: "Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after this" moves John from the churches on earth to the throne room, so that he and his readers see the coming troubles from where God rules. The words echo Daniel 2:28–29 in the Greek. For the churches, the call means that what follows is shown from heaven's side.
views: Many dispensationalists (Scofield, Walvoord) read the call as a picture of the church caught up before the tribulation, noting that "church" does not appear again until 22:16. Others answer that the words are spoken to John alone, who is "in the Spirit" (4:2), and that the same call comes to the two witnesses in 11:12. See the card at 3:10.

settings.what: The songs around the throne
settings.by: the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders
settings.to: God on the throne; overheard by John and, through him, by the seven churches
settings.when: in John's vision of heaven, after the door is opened
settings.why: The first hymns of heaven say who is truly worthy of worship. The elders lay down their crowns, as client kings bowed before the emperor, and they say "You are worthy, our Lord and God," words like the title "Lord and God" that Suetonius says Domitian liked to hear (that echo assumes the later date). For churches pressed to honor Caesar, the songs declare that only the Creator deserves it. The churches probably sang hymns like these in their own worship.
views: A protest against the emperor cult
Many scholars read these hymns as a deliberate answer to the court ceremony and titles of the emperor.
Others stress that the songs come from Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 and Jewish worship, whatever echo of Rome they carry.

title: The Scroll and the Lamb
sum: God holds a scroll sealed with seven seals. No one is worthy to open it, and John weeps. An elder tells him that "the Lion from the tribe of Judah" has won the victory (5:5). John looks, and instead of a lion he sees a Lamb that looks as though he had been slaughtered. The Lamb takes the scroll, and all of creation, every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and on the sea, sings to God and to the Lamb.
This is the hinge of the whole book. John hears "Lion" and sees "Lamb." The power that rules history is a sacrifice.

readings: Read literally
A real scroll in heaven that only Christ can open. Its seals begin the events of chapter 6.
Read as symbol
Seven horns mean full power, seven eyes full knowledge. The Lamb "standing" yet "slaughtered" is the risen Christ who still bears his wounds. Revelation uses "Lamb" for Jesus 28 times.

views.P: The scroll is God's verdict on unfaithful Jerusalem. Some compare it to a certificate of divorce.
views.H: The scroll holds the history of the church to the end of the age.
views.F: The scroll is like the title deed to the earth. Opening it starts the future tribulation.
views.I: Christ's death and resurrection is the key that unlocks the meaning of all history.

deep.b:
The widening circles of praise

VersesWho singsTo whomWhat they say
5:8–10The four creatures and 24 elders, with harps and incenseThe LambA new song: "You are worthy... because you were slaughtered"
5:11–12Angels, "myriads of myriads" (Daniel 7:10)The LambA sevenfold praise: power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory and blessing
5:13Every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the seaGod and the Lamb togetherA fourfold praise: blessing, honor, glory and power "forever and ever"
5:14The four creatures, then the elders—"Amen," and they fall down and worship

Four is the number of the world (four winds, four corners), seven the number of completeness. The praise starts at the throne and spreads until it fills all creation.

The sealed scroll

The scroll has "writing inside and on the back" (5:1), like the scroll Ezekiel was given, written front and back with laments, mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Sealed documents in the Roman world included wills and contracts, and one form of Roman will was sealed by seven witnesses (Gaius, Institutes 2.119). Daniel was told to keep the book sealed until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4). Many readers see the scroll as God's plan for history, which only the Lamb can put into effect; others as the deed to the world, a last will, or the Old Testament itself, unlocked by Christ.

A lamb with horns

A lamb with seven horns sounds strange, but horns meant power (Daniel 7:7–8; 8:3). In 1 Enoch's "Animal Apocalypse," written about 160 BC, God's people are a flock of sheep; lambs among them grow horns, and one grows a great horn and fights for the flock (1 Enoch 90:9–12). John's Lamb has that power, complete (seven horns), but he has it "as though slaughtered."

echoes: Genesis 49:9–10; Isaiah 11:1, 10; Isaiah 53:7; Exodus 12; Ezekiel 2:9–10; Daniel 7:10

settings.what: The angel's question and the elder's comfort
settings.by: a mighty angel, then one of the elders
settings.to: all creation, then John, who is weeping
settings.when: when no one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll
settings.why: The angel asks "Who is worthy to open the scroll and to break its seals?" The elder tells John "Stop weeping." and points to the Lion of Judah. John then sees a slaughtered Lamb. For the churches, the Messiah they hoped for wins not by force but by dying, and that is the pattern for their own victory.

settings.what: The new song to the Lamb
settings.by: the living creatures and the elders, then many angels, then every creature
settings.to: the Lamb who was slaughtered, and God on the throne
settings.when: after the Lamb takes the sealed scroll
settings.why: The hymn explains why the Lamb can open the scroll: not by force but because he was killed and bought people "from every tribe and language and people and nation." For small house churches, the song says that they belong to a worldwide kingdom of priests, and that victory comes the way the Lamb won it, by faithful suffering. The circle of praise grows until all creation joins.

traditions.q: The elders hold gold bowls full of incense, "These are the prayers of the saints" (5:8; see 6:9–10 and 8:3–4). Do the saints in heaven pray for us, and may we ask them to?
views: Yes. The saints in heaven are alive in Christ, care for those still on earth and pray for them, so it is good to ask their prayers, as you would ask a friend's (Catechism 956, 2683). Scenes like this one show heaven taking part in the prayers of the church. Catholic writers also point to 2 Maccabees 15:12–14, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches only (not for Protestants or Jews), where Judas dreams that Onias, the dead high priest, "was praying for the whole Jewish community" (2 Maccabees 15:12), and that Onias calls Jeremiah "the one who prays much for the people and the holy city" (2 Maccabees 15:14).

Yes. Asking the Mother of God and the saints to pray for us belongs to every service, and incense rises in Orthodox worship as it does before the throne here. The church in heaven and on earth is one family at prayer.

The saints do pray for the church, but we should not pray to them. The Augsburg Confession (article 21) says the saints should be remembered as examples of faith, but Scripture does not teach calling on them, since Christ is the one mediator.
Divided. The Thirty-Nine Articles (article 22) reject the invocation of saints, and many Anglicans follow that, while Anglo-Catholics ask the saints' prayers much as Catholics do.

No. The Westminster Confession says prayer is to be made to God alone, not to angels or saints. The bowls hold the prayers of believers on earth, which come before God through Christ, and the scene does not show anyone praying to the elders.

title: Six Seals and Four Riders
sum: The Lamb opens the seals one at a time. The first four release four horsemen: a white horse whose rider has a bow and a crown, a red horse whose rider has a huge sword, a black horse whose rider holds a balance scale, and a pale green horse ridden by Death, with Hades following.

The fifth seal shows the souls of those who were slaughtered for God's word, under the altar, crying, "How long?" The sixth seal brings a great earthquake: the sun goes black, the moon becomes like blood, and the powerful hide in caves, asking, "Who is able to stand?"

readings: Read literally
Real wars, famines and plagues, coming one after another, and real signs in the sky.
Read as symbol

The horsemen come from Zechariah 1 and 6 and match what Jesus said in Matthew 24: wars, famines and earthquakes, "only the start of the labor pains" (Matthew 24:8). "The sun turned black" is the prophets' normal way of describing the fall of a kingdom (Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4).

views.P: Rome's war on Judea, AD 66–70, including the terrible famine of the siege recorded by Josephus.
views.H: The Roman Empire's history from about AD 96 to 313, ending with the fall of pagan Rome.
views.F: The first half of a future tribulation. The white rider is the Antichrist offering false peace.
views.I: These forces run through every age, and Christ holds the reins of each one.

deep.b:
The six seals

SealWhat appearsSourceCommon readings
1 (6:1–2)White horse; rider with a bow and crownZechariah 1:8; Zechariah 6:1–3Conquest; Parthian invaders; Christ and the gospel; a false christ
2 (6:3–4)Red horse; rider with a huge swordZechariah 6:2War and civil war
3 (6:5–6)Black horse; rider with scalesEzekiel 4:16Famine and inflation
4 (6:7–8)Pale green horse; Death, with Hades followingEzekiel 14:21Death by sword, famine, disease and wild animals, over a fourth of the earth
5 (6:9–11)Souls under the altar: "How long?"Leviticus 4:7; Psalm 79:5; Psalm 79:10Martyrs waiting for justice
6 (6:12–17)Earthquake, black sun, falling starsIsaiah 34:4; Joel 2:31; Hosea 10:8The day of the Lord; the collapse of a world order

Jesus’s list of "labor pains" in Matthew 24:6–8 runs in nearly the same order: wars, nations at war, famines, earthquakes, then persecution (Matthew 24:9) and signs in the sky (Matthew 24:29).

A day’s wages for a quart of wheat

A choinix (about a quart) of wheat was one man's daily ration; a denarius was a day's wage. That price is roughly ten times normal, by the estimates commentators draw from grain prices recorded elsewhere in the empire: a worker could feed himself but not his family. Barley, the poor man's grain, buys three times as much. "Leave the oil and the wine unharmed" may point to a real event: about AD 92 Domitian ordered half the vineyards in the provinces cut down to grow more grain, and then let the order drop (Suetonius, Domitian 7.2 and 14.2); later writers say cities in Asia sent envoys to protest. Whatever the background, the luxury crops survive while bread runs short.

The archer on the white horse

The only rider with a bow was a fearful image to Romans. The Parthians, Rome's enemies beyond the Euphrates, were famous mounted archers and they destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC and forced another to surrender in AD 62. A conquering bowman from the east was the empire's nightmare, which is why many read the first seal as invasion rather than as Christ.

Who is the white rider? Three answers: Christ and the gospel going out (compare 19:11); a false Christ imitating him; or the Parthians, mounted archers from the east and the one empire Rome feared. Each horseman is "given" his power, so all four answer to the Lamb.

The Jewish historian Josephus, an eyewitness, describes the famine in Jerusalem during the Roman siege of AD 70: people ate leather and grass, and grain was sold secretly at huge prices (Jewish War 5.10; 6.3). Preterists read the black horse against that background.

deep.title: Fimbulwinter before Ragnarök
deep.b: In Norse myth the end of the world is preceded by Fimbulwinter: three winters with no summer, while brothers kill each other in war. Then wolves swallow the sun and the moon, and the stars fall (Völuspá; Snorri's Gylfaginning). War, hunger and a darkened sky before the end closely match the seals. These Norse sources were written down around 1200, by Christians, so some borrowing may run the other way.

echoes: Zechariah 1:8; Zechariah 6:1–8; Ezekiel 14:21; Matthew 24:6–8; Isaiah 34:4; Hosea 10:8

settings.what: The four commands "Come!" and the voice among the living creatures
settings.by: each of the four living creatures in turn; then a voice from among them (6:6)
settings.to: the four riders, or John (see the views)
settings.when: as the Lamb opens the first four seals
settings.why: Each of the four living creatures around God's throne (4:6–8) gives the word that sends a rider out, so the war, famine and death that follow go out only when heaven allows. The voice that sets famine prices (6:6) also sets a limit: grain is scarce, but the oil and the wine are spared, and Death's authority reaches only a quarter of the earth. For churches living under Roman power, the scene says that even the empire's disasters are on a leash.
views: Most modern commentators read "Come!" as a summons to each horseman to ride out. The oldest manuscripts have the single word.
The later reading "Come and see!" (KJV) makes the command an invitation to John to come and look (see the variant at 6:1).

settings.what: The martyrs' prayer and the answer
settings.by: the souls under the altar of those slaughtered for God's word; then a reply from heaven
settings.to: God, "Master, holy and true"
settings.when: when the Lamb breaks the fifth seal
settings.why: The martyrs ask "how long" until God judges, a cry from the psalms. They are given white robes and told to rest a little while longer, because more will be killed. For churches that knew of Antipas's death and feared more, the answer is honest: suffering is not over yet, but God has heard, and the dead are safe with him. Later scenes answer this prayer: the voice from the altar at the sixth trumpet (9:13), the angel's oath that there will be no more waiting (10:6), and the songs of 16:5–7 and 19:2.
views: Some readers find the prayer vengeful. Others note that it asks God, not the church, to act, and that it is a plea for justice like those in the psalms.

settings.what: The cry of the kings to the mountains
settings.by: the kings, rulers, generals, the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person
settings.to: the mountains and rocks
settings.when: at the opening of the sixth seal, as the sky and earth are shaken
settings.why: The powerful people who seemed safe now hide, saying "Fall on us! Hide us," words from Hosea 10:8. Their question, "who is able to stand?", is answered in chapter 7: the sealed and the crowd in white stand before the throne. For small churches under the rule of the powerful, it shows that no rank protects anyone before God.

traditions.q: The souls under the altar are aware, cry out to God, and are told to rest a little while longer (6:9–11). Are the dead conscious and with God before the resurrection?
views: Yes. The souls of the just who die in God's grace are with Christ before the resurrection and see God (Catechism 1023–1029); the martyrs above all are honored as already in glory. The old custom of placing martyrs' relics in or beneath altars is often linked with this verse.

Yes. The departed live in Christ and have a foretaste of joy or sorrow until the final judgment (Confession of Dositheus, decree 18). The martyrs' cry shows that the saints in heaven know what happens on earth and pray, one ground for asking their prayers; Orthodox altars hold the relics of martyrs.

Luther often spoke of death as a sleep, but Lutheran teaching holds that believers' souls are with Christ while they await the resurrection. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession grants that the saints in heaven pray for the church in general, while rejecting prayers addressed to them.

At death the souls of believers, "which neither die nor sleep," return to God and wait in heaven for the redemption of their bodies (Westminster Confession 32.1). The robed, speaking souls of 6:9–11 are read as a true picture of that waiting.
The same as the Reformed view: believers' souls go at once to be with Christ, and their bodies rest until the resurrection (Second London Confession 31.1).

Death is an unconscious sleep until the resurrection (Fundamental Belief 26). The scene is symbolic: like Abel's blood crying out from the ground (Genesis 4:10), the martyrs' blood at the altar calls for justice; it does not show conscious souls in heaven.

Humans have no soul that survives death, and the dead are conscious of nothing. The "souls" are the martyrs' lives, poured out like sacrificial blood at the base of the altar and calling for justice as Abel's blood did.

title: The 144,000 and the Countless Crowd
sum: Four angels hold back the four winds. Another angel seals the slaves of God on their foreheads: 144,000, which is 12,000 from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Then John looks and sees a crowd so large that no one could count it, from every nation, tribe, people and language, in white robes, holding palm branches. They are "the ones who are coming out of the great suffering."

The pattern from chapter 5 repeats. There John heard "Lion" and saw a Lamb. Here he hears a number from Israel and sees a crowd from every nation. Whether these are two groups or one group seen two ways is the center of the Church and Israel question.

readings: Read literally
The 144,000 are Jewish believers, 12,000 from each tribe, sealed during the tribulation. The crowd is a second group: people from the nations saved during that time.
Read as symbol

144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000: the tribes times the apostles times a great number, all of God's people. The list reads like a military census (Numbers 1). The uncountable crowd fulfills God's promise that Abraham's family would be as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5).

views.P: The 144,000 are Jewish Christians who escaped Jerusalem before AD 70.
views.H: The true church, sealed and kept during the barbarian invasions (the four winds).
views.F: A literal remnant of Israel, plus a great crowd of people saved during the tribulation.
views.I: The whole church, protected spiritually but not physically, as it passes through suffering.

deep.b:
The tribes in 7:5–8

Revelation 7 orderNotes
JudahFirst, not Reuben the firstborn: the tribe of the Messiah (5:5)
Reuben, Gad, Asher, NaphtaliFour sons of Leah, Zilpah and Bilhah, mixed together
ManassehJoseph’s son, listed although Joseph also appears
Simeon, Levi, Issachar, ZebulunFour sons of Leah; Levi, the priestly tribe with no land, is counted
Joseph, BenjaminRachel’s sons come last
Missing: Dan and EphraimBoth linked with idols (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29–30; Hosea 4:17)

There are about 20 different tribe lists in the Old Testament, and none matches this one. Irenaeus (about AD 180) thought Dan was left out because the Antichrist would come from it (Against Heresies 5.30.2), reading Jeremiah 8:16.

Palm branches and shelter

The great crowd holds palm branches (7:9), the sign of the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40), when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness. God "will shelter them" (7:15, literally "will pitch his tent over them"). Zechariah says that one day the nations will come up to Jerusalem to keep this feast (Zechariah 14:16). Crowds also waved palms when Jesus entered Jerusalem (John 12:13).

Every tear wiped away

7:16–17 combines three promises: "They will not go hungry or thirsty; no scorching wind or sun will strike them" (Isaiah 49:10); "The Lord GOD will wipe the tears off every face" (Isaiah 25:8); and the Lamb will be their shepherd (Ezekiel 34:23; Psalm 23). The Lamb becomes the shepherd: the one who was led to slaughter now leads the flock.
Jehovah's Witnesses read the 144,000 literally: only that many go to heaven to rule with Christ, while other faithful people live forever on a restored earth.
The church historian Eusebius (about AD 325) says the Christians of Jerusalem were warned by a prophecy and fled to Pella, east of the Jordan, before the city fell (Church History 3.5.3).

The tribe list is unusual. Judah is listed first, not Reuben the firstborn. Dan and Ephraim are missing. Both Joseph and his son Manasseh are listed, and Levi, normally given no land, is included. Both are tied to the golden calves: Jeroboam, an Ephraimite, set one calf up at Dan and the other at Bethel, a town on the border of Benjamin and Ephraim (1 Kings 11:26; 1 Kings 12:28–30), and Hosea calls Ephraim "joined to idols" (Hosea 4:17). That link may explain why they are left out.

deep.title: Dan is missing here, but first in line at the end
deep.b: Dan is left out of the sealing in chapter 7. But in Ezekiel's vision of restored Israel, Dan is the very first tribe given land (Ezekiel 48:1) and has its own gate in the city (Ezekiel 48:32). Revelation 21 openly borrows Ezekiel's city, with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes, and it never lists which tribes. I suspect Dan's absence in chapter 7 is a mark of judgment on idolatry for that period, not a final exclusion. The worst tribe still gets a gate. The early idea that the Antichrist comes from Dan (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30) is old, but Revelation never says it.

echoes: Ezekiel 9:4; Numbers 1–2; Genesis 15:5; Leviticus 23:40; Isaiah 49:10; Isaiah 25:8

settings.what: The command to seal the slaves of God
settings.by: an angel with the seal of the living God
settings.to: the four angels holding back the winds
settings.when: between the sixth and seventh seals
settings.why: Before harm comes, God marks his own. The scene draws on Ezekiel 9, where those who grieve over the city's sins are marked before judgment. For the churches, it says God protects his people through the trouble, not that they escape all suffering.

settings.what: The crowd's praise, the angels' praise, and the elder's answer
settings.by: the crowd from every nation (7:10); the angels, the elders and the living creatures (7:11–12); one of the elders, in dialogue with John (7:13–17)
settings.to: God and the Lamb (7:10–12); John (7:13–17)
settings.when: between the sixth and seventh seals, after the sealing of the 144,000
settings.why: The vision answers the question at the end of chapter 6, "who is able to stand?" The crowd in white are "the ones who are coming out of the great suffering." For churches facing poverty and prison, the elder's words promise shelter, no more hunger or thirst, and that "God will wipe every tear from their eyes."
views: Some read the crowd as the martyrs; others as the whole church, or the 144,000 seen from another side.

Preterists link it to the trials of the first century, futurists to a coming tribulation, historicists to the trials of the church through its history, such as the persecutions under the later emperors, and idealists to the suffering of the church in every age.

traditions.q: Who are the 144,000 sealed "from all the tribes of Israel" (7:4; 14:1–5), and how do they relate to the great crowd (7:9)?
views: The number is literal. The 144,000 are anointed Christians chosen since Pentecost who will rule with Christ in heaven, while the great crowd are faithful people who will live forever on a restored earth; only the anointed eat the bread and drink the wine at the yearly Memorial.

They are 12,000 Jews from each tribe of Israel, sealed during the future tribulation after the church has been raptured. Many teachers think they will preach during that time, and the great crowd are people saved through their witness.

Early Adventists linked the 144,000 to the faithful who are alive when Christ returns. Ellen White warned members not to argue about who they will be, and Adventists today hold several views, many taking the number as symbolic.

The number is a symbol: twelve tribes times twelve times a thousand, the complete people of God built on Israel and the apostles. The Catechism counts the 144,000 as the new People of God in heaven's worship, alongside the great crowd from every nation (Catechism 1138). Catholic writers differ on whether the two groups are one, and the Church reads this chapter on All Saints' Day.

The 144,000 and the great crowd are one group. John hears a number and then sees a crowd, just as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5–6): the church is the true Israel, counted and complete, yet too many to count.

title: Silence, Incense and Four Trumpets
sum: The seventh seal brings silence in heaven for about half an hour. Seven angels receive trumpets. Another angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints on the gold altar, then fills the incense pan with fire and throws it onto the earth.

The first four trumpets strike a third of the land, the sea, the fresh water and the sky: hail and fire mixed with blood, a burning mountain thrown into the sea, a star named Wormwood that makes the water bitter, and a darkened sun, moon and stars. An eagle cries, "Woe, woe, woe!"

readings: Read literally
Real future disasters to nature. Some modern readers have suggested meteor impacts, volcanic eruptions or nuclear fallout. Many note that the name Chernobyl comes from a plant related to wormwood.
Read as symbol

The trumpets replay the plagues of Egypt: hail and fire (the 7th plague), water to blood (the 1st), darkness (the 9th). Only "a third" is struck, so these are warnings. They answer the martyrs' prayers of 6:10, which rise with the incense.

views.P: The Roman armies and the warring rebel factions inside Judea during the Jewish War.
views.H: The barbarian invasions of the Western Roman Empire: Goths, Vandals, Huns, and the fall of Rome in 476.
views.F: Future judgments during the tribulation, many taken literally.
views.I: Natural and spiritual disasters through history, each one a call to turn back to God.

deep.b:
The first four trumpets and Egypt’s plagues

TrumpetWhat happensExodus parallel
1 (8:7)Hail and fire mixed with blood; a third of the land and trees burnedThe seventh plague, hail with fire (Exodus 9:23–25)
2 (8:8–9)A burning mountain thrown into the sea; a third of the sea becomes bloodThe first plague, the Nile turned to blood (Exodus 7:20–21)
3 (8:10–11)A star named Wormwood falls; a third of the rivers turn bitterBitter water at Marah (Exodus 15:23); Jeremiah 9:15
4 (8:12)A third of the sun, moon and stars darkenedThe ninth plague, darkness (Exodus 10:21–23)

Some modern scholars connect the burning mountain thrown into the sea with Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii in AD 79; the Sibylline Oracles (book 4) treat that eruption as divine judgment.

Silence, then trumpets

"Silence in heaven for about half an hour" (8:1) echoes the prophets. Zephaniah 1:7 commands silence before the Lord GOD, because the day of the LORD is near (see also Habakkuk 2:20; Zechariah 2:13). In Israel, silver trumpets called the people to gather, to march, to battle and to festivals (Numbers 10:1–10), and at Jericho seven priests blew seven trumpets before the walls fell (Joshua 6). Trumpets in Revelation are both warning and battle signal.

Wormwood and Chernobyl

Wormwood (apsinthos) is a bitter plant, used by the prophets for the bitterness of judgment (Jeremiah 9:15; Lamentations 3:15). After the 1986 nuclear disaster, many noted that "Chornobyl" is the Ukrainian name of a related plant, mugwort. It is a striking coincidence, though the two plants are different species and Revelation is describing a star, not a reactor.

echoes: Exodus 9:23–25; Exodus 7:20; Exodus 10:21–23; Jeremiah 9:15; Joel 2:1; Leviticus 16:12–13

settings.what: The eagle's threefold woe
settings.by: an eagle flying high overhead
settings.to: "the people who live on the earth"
settings.when: after the first four trumpets
settings.why: The cry warns that the last three trumpets will be worse. In Revelation "the people who live on the earth" usually means those who side with the beast against God's people. For the churches, the warning shows that the trumpets are calls to repent before it is too late (9:20–21).

title: Locusts and the Army from the Euphrates
sum: The fifth trumpet opens the abyss. Locusts pour out with the smoke, shaped like war horses, with human faces, long hair, lions' teeth and scorpion tails. They may hurt but not kill, for five months, and only those without God's seal. Their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek: "Destruction" and "Destroyer."

The sixth trumpet releases four angels at the Euphrates and an army of 200 million riders on lion-headed horses that breathe fire. A third of the human race dies. The chapter's real point is its last line: the survivors still did not repent of their idols, murders, magic, sexual immorality or thefts.

readings: Read literally
Real demonic or military forces in the future. Popular teachers have suggested attack helicopters for the locusts and a modern Asian army for the 200 million.
Read as symbol

The locusts come from Joel 1–2, where a locust plague is pictured as an invading army that looks like horses and has a lion's teeth. The Euphrates was Israel's ancient border and the edge of the Roman Empire, the direction invaders came from.

views.P: Rebel factions and Roman troops during the Jewish War; some read "five months" as the summer of AD 66 or the siege months of AD 70.
views.H: The classic Protestant reading: the locusts are the Arab armies of the 600s–700s (five months read as 150 years); the 6th trumpet is the Ottoman Turks, who took Constantinople in 1453.
views.F: A future demonic invasion and a vast army, perhaps literal.
views.I: Spiritual torment and the self-destruction that come with idolatry in every age.

deep.b:
Locusts from Joel

Revelation 9Joel
Locusts like horses made ready for war (9:7)They look like horses and run like horsemen (Joel 2:4)
Teeth like a lion’s (9:8)The invading swarm has a lion’s teeth (Joel 1:6)
Wings sound like many chariots (9:9)A sound like chariots leaping over the hilltops (Joel 2:5)
The sun and air darkened by smoke (9:2)Sun and moon grow dark (Joel 2:10)
A king over them (9:11)"Locusts have no king" (Proverbs 30:27)

A locust swarm can cover hundreds of square miles and eat its own weight in plants every day. In the ancient world it meant famine.

Two hundred million and the Euphrates

The Euphrates was the eastern edge of the Roman Empire; beyond it lay Parthia. The number of riders is two hundred million (9:16), in Greek literally "double myriads of myriads," a number meant to overwhelm, larger than every army of the ancient world put together. In 1970 Hal Lindsey linked it to a Chinese claim of a 200-million-strong militia, and others have linked it to demonic forces or to the countless dead of history's wars. Its horses have lions' heads and tails like snakes, more like monsters than cavalry.

"They did not repent"

The chapter ends with a list of what people refused to give up: worshiping demons and idols "that cannot see or hear or walk" (9:20; compare Psalm 115:4–7), murder, magic, sexual sin and theft (9:20–21). The word for magic is pharmaka, the root of our "pharmacy": the potions, poisons and charms of sorcery. The Byzantine text and the KJV have the related pharmakeia, "sorceries," the word used for Babylon in 18:23.
Apollyon sounds like Apollo, the god that emperors such as Nero and Domitian liked to be linked with. Some scholars think John is making a pointed joke: Rome's favorite god is the king of the pit.

echoes: Joel 1:6; Joel 2:4–10; Exodus 10:12–15; Job 26:6; Genesis 15:18; Isaiah 2:20

settings.what: The voice from the altar: "Untie the four angels"
settings.by: a single voice from the horns of the gold altar before God
settings.to: the sixth angel, the one holding the trumpet
settings.when: when the sixth trumpet sounds
settings.why: The command comes from the gold altar where the prayers of the saints went up with the incense (8:3–5), the altar under which the martyrs cried "How long?" (6:9–10). The sixth trumpet is heaven's answer to those prayers, and the altar speaks again in 16:7. For persecuted churches it meant their prayers were not lost: they reached God's altar, and the altar answered. The answer is still limited, a third of the human race, and its aim is repentance, which the survivors refuse (9:20–21).

title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
sum: A mighty angel comes down dressed in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head, a face like the sun and feet like pillars of fire. He stands with one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a small open scroll. Seven thunders speak, but John is told to keep what they said under seal.

The angel raises his hand and swears, "There will be no more waiting!" When the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God that he told as good news to the prophets will be finished. John eats the little scroll. It tastes sweet as honey but makes his stomach bitter, and he is told to prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.

readings: Read literally
A real angel and a real message, with the seven thunders kept secret until the end.
Read as symbol

John is given his calling the way Ezekiel was: he eats the scroll (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3). God's word is sweet to receive and bitter to deliver. The angel's oath answers Daniel 12:7, where an angel swears how long the waiting would last.

views.P: John is commissioned to announce the coming fall of Jerusalem.
views.H: The opened little scroll is the Bible given back to the people at the Reformation.
views.F: A pause before the final trumpet and the last half of the tribulation.
views.I: Every faithful witness finds God's word both sweet and bitter.

deep.b:
The mighty angel

FeatureWhere else it appears
Wrapped in a cloud (10:1)Jesus comes "with the clouds" (1:7); God led Israel in a cloud (Exodus 13:21)
A rainbow over his head (10:1)The rainbow around God’s throne (4:3)
Face like the sun (10:1)The risen Jesus (1:16)
Feet like pillars of fire (10:1)The pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21); the risen Jesus’s glowing feet (1:15)
One foot on the sea, one on the land (10:2)His message is for the whole world
A voice like a lion’s roar (10:3)Amos 3:8: the lion has roared, and the Lord GOD has spoken
Raises his hand to heaven and swears (10:5–6)The man in linen in Daniel 12:7 raises both hands and swears by the one who lives forever that it will be for a time, times and half a time

Because he looks so much like Jesus in chapter 1, some interpreters think the angel is Christ himself, or the Angel of the LORD: many older historicists, and in recent times the Reformed commentator G. K. Beale. Most think he is a great angel who carries Christ’s glory.

"No more waiting," not "no more time"

The KJV has the angel swear "that there should be time no longer" (10:6, KJV), which became a popular saying about the end of time itself. The Greek chronos ouketi estai means there will be no more delay or waiting, as nearly all modern translations take it. It answers the martyrs' cry "How long?" (6:10).

Seven thunders, and a scroll to eat

The seven thunders are the only thing in the book John is told not to write down (10:4). Psalm 29 calls thunder "the voice of the LORD" seven times. Then John eats a little scroll, as Ezekiel did (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3; also Jeremiah 15:16): sweet in his mouth, bitter in his stomach (10:9–10), the same bitterness as the waters of Wormwood (8:11). God's message is good news, the angel calls it that (10:7), and also a hard word to carry.

echoes: Ezekiel 2:8–3:3; Daniel 12:4–9; Psalm 29:3–9; Amos 3:7; Jeremiah 15:16

settings.what: The angel's oath and John's new call
settings.by: a mighty angel, a voice from heaven, and then a voice telling John to prophesy
settings.to: John, and through him the churches
settings.when: between the sixth and seventh trumpets
settings.why: The angel swears, "There will be no more waiting!" John eats the little scroll, sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, as Ezekiel ate his scroll. Then he is told, "Once more you must prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings." The second half of the book is framed as a message about the nations, and the bitter taste warns the churches that their witness will cost them.
views: Some take it as the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5; Bauckham notes that in 10:8 the best text calls it simply "the scroll" (see the variant). Others take it as a smaller message: the content of chapter 11, or of chapters 11–22.

title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
sum: John measures God's temple, but the outer court is given to the nations, who trample the holy city for 42 months. Two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days. Like Elijah and Moses, they shut the sky and turn water into blood. The beast from the abyss kills them, and their corpse lies in the street of "the great city... where their Lord too was crucified." After 3½ days they rise, hear "Come up here!", and go up to heaven.
Then the seventh trumpet sounds: "The kingdom of the world has become our Lord's and his Messiah's." God's temple in heaven opens, and the ark of the covenant is seen.
