readings: Read literally

A rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, and two individual prophets, perhaps Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah, the two who never died. Some note that the whole world watching their bodies fits modern media.
Read as symbol

The temple is God's people (1 Corinthians 3:16), and measuring it means protecting it. The two witnesses are called "two lampstands," and 1:20 already said lampstands are churches. There are two because the Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

views.P: The Jerusalem temple before AD 70. "The great city where their Lord was crucified" is Jerusalem, and the 42 months match the Roman war.
views.H: The witnesses are the Old and New Testaments, or faithful groups such as the Waldensians.
views.F: Two prophets in a rebuilt Jerusalem temple during the tribulation.
views.I: The church's witness, suffering, and final vindication in every age.

deep.b:
Three and a half, five ways

PhraseWhereWho or what
42 months11:2; 13:5The nations trample the holy city; the beast has authority
1,260 days11:3; 12:6The two witnesses prophesy; the woman is kept in the wilderness
"A time, times and half a time"12:14The woman is kept safe (from Daniel 7:25; 12:7)
3½ days11:9, 11The witnesses’ bodies lie in the street
3½ years of droughtLuke 4:25; James 5:17The drought in Elijah’s day, which the witnesses’ power recalls (11:6)

Half of seven: a broken, limited period. The same span is both the time of trampling and the time of protected witness.

Who are the two witnesses?

ProposalWhyHeld by
Moses and ElijahThey turn water to blood and shut the sky (Exodus 7; 1 Kings 17:1); both appear at the TransfigurationMany futurists
Enoch and ElijahThe two who never died (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11)Tertullian, Hippolytus and much of the early church
Peter and PaulKilled in Rome under NeroSome preterists
The witnessing churchThey are called "two lampstands" (11:4), and lampstands are churches (1:20); the law needs two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15)Many idealists and scholars
The Old and New TestamentsGod’s two witnesses in writing; their "death" and rising were read as the attack on the Bible in the French Revolution and its recoveryMany historicists, including Ellen White (The Great Controversy, ch. 15)

Measuring the temple

John is told to measure the temple and the altar but leave out the outer court (11:1–2). Ezekiel watched an angel measure a future temple (Ezekiel 40–42), and Zechariah saw a man measuring Jerusalem (Zechariah 2:1–5). Measuring marks something as God's and protected. Futurists see a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem; preterists the temple before AD 70; many others the church, which Paul calls God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Moses and Elijah appear together with Jesus at the Transfiguration (Mark 9:4), which is one reason many readers name them as the two witnesses. Malachi 4:5 also promises that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.

deep.title: The two witnesses as Israel and the church, standing side by side
deep.b: Three passages use olive trees for God's people. In Zechariah 4, two olive trees feed one lampstand: the king and the priest of restored Israel. In Romans 11, Paul pictures one olive tree with natural branches (Israel) and grafted branches (the nations). Revelation 11 has two olive trees and two lampstands. Seven lampstands meant the whole church in chapter 1. My speculation is that the two lampstands are the two branches of Paul's tree, believing Israel and the church from the nations, witnessing together as the "kingdom of priests" (1:6). That would explain why there are two, why they share one story of death and resurrection, and why they appear in Jerusalem. I have not seen this argued in the main commentaries, though someone may have suggested it.

echoes: Zechariah 4:2–14; Ezekiel 40–42; 1 Kings 17:1; Exodus 7:17–20; Ezekiel 37:10; Daniel 7:14; 2 Kings 2:11; Psalm 2:1–9; Psalm 99:1; Esther 9:19–22

settings.what: The command to measure the temple
settings.by: a voice speaking to John
settings.to: John
settings.when: just after he is told to prophesy again
settings.why: John is to measure the temple, the altar and the people who worship in it, but to leave out the outer court, handed over to the nations for 42 months. The measuring marks God's people as protected in their worship even while the city is trampled. Then God promises to let his two witnesses prophesy. For the churches, the scene pictures their role: to witness in a hostile world.
views: Early-date scholars and preterists read this as the Jerusalem temple before AD 70, so it helps date the book.
Most late-date scholars read the temple as God's people, as Paul uses the image in 1 Corinthians 3:16.
Futurists often expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem.
Historicists have read the 42 months as 1,260 years of church history, often of papal power.

settings.what: "Come up here!"
settings.by: a great voice from heaven
settings.to: the two witnesses, while their enemies look on
settings.when: after they rise, three and a half days after their death
settings.why: The same call John heard in 4:1 now lifts the witnesses into heaven in the cloud, in full view of their enemies, the way Jesus was raised and taken up (Acts 1:9). Their defeat is overturned in public. For churches facing death for their witness, it promised that God would vindicate them before the very people who mocked them.
views: Mid-tribulation readers see the church caught up here, before the last trumpet (see the note on 11:12).
Most others read a picture of resurrection and vindication, modeled on Jesus's own.

settings.what: The proclamation at the seventh trumpet
settings.by: loud voices in heaven
settings.to: heaven and earth: a public announcement, heard by John
settings.when: when the seventh angel blows his trumpet
settings.why: Heaven announces the end before the book has shown it: "The kingdom of the world has become our Lord's and his Messiah's." The words come from Psalm 2, where the nations rise against the LORD and his anointed. The churches lived in the kingdom of the world ruled by Rome. The proclamation tells them that the change of rule is certain.

settings.what: The elders' thanksgiving
settings.by: the twenty-four elders
settings.to: God, the Lord God, the Almighty
settings.when: right after the proclamation of 11:15
settings.why: The elders thank God that he has taken up his reign, and say what that means: the nations' fury is met by God's, the dead are judged, the reward is given to his slaves the prophets, to the saints and to all who fear his name, small and great, and those who destroy the earth are destroyed. God is no longer called the one "who is coming": he has come. For churches that feared Rome, the song promised that their small faithfulness would be rewarded, and that the powers ruining the world would answer for it.

title: The Woman, the Child and the Dragon
sum: A great sign appears in heaven: a woman wrapped in the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and twelve stars as a crown, about to give birth. A great fiery-red dragon with seven crowned heads and ten horns waits to devour her child. She gives birth to a son who will shepherd the nations, and the child is snatched up to God's throne. The woman flees into the wilderness for 1,260 days.

War breaks out in heaven. Michael's angels throw the dragon down, and he is named plainly: "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan." God's people win the victory over him "because of the blood of the Lamb" and their testimony. This chapter steps behind the scenes to show the real enemy behind the beasts that come next.

readings: Read literally

Some readers tie 12:1–2 to a real arrangement of stars in the constellation Virgo. Predictions built on this, such as the one for September 23, 2017, did not come true. Most literal readers still read the woman as a symbol of national Israel.
Read as symbol

The woman is Israel (in Joseph's dream the sun, moon and stars are Jacob's family, Genesis 37:9), who gives birth to the Messiah, and then the faithful people of God. Christian tradition also sees Mary here, and Eve, since the "ancient serpent" fights the woman's offspring (Genesis 3:15).

views.P: Israel gives birth to the Messiah. The woman's flight is the Jerusalem church escaping before AD 70.
views.H: The true church in the wilderness during 1,260 years of persecution, often dated AD 538–1798.
views.F: The woman is national Israel, protected for the last 3½ years.
views.I: The age-long war between God's people and Satan, from Eden to the end.

deep.b:
The cast

FigureDescriptionMain identifications
The womanWrapped in the sun, moon beneath her feet, crown of 12 stars (12:1)Israel (Genesis 37:9); Mary; the people of God from which Messiah comes; the church
The male childWill shepherd the nations with an iron rod; snatched up to God (12:5)The Messiah (Psalm 2:9); Jesus’s birth and ascension
The dragonFiery red, seven heads, ten horns, drags away a third of the stars (12:3–4)"The ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (12:9)
MichaelLeads the angels against the dragon (12:7)Israel’s guardian angel (Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:21; Daniel 12:1)
The woman’s other children"Those who keep the commandments of God and hold on to the testimony of Jesus" (12:17)Believers; for Adventists, the last-days remnant (see the note on 12:17)

A baby god among seven stars

In AD 83 Domitian's infant son died, and the emperor declared him a god. Coins struck for his wife Domitia show the child as a baby god seated on a globe, reaching up to seven stars. For John's readers, Rome had its own story of a divine child and a mother honored as "mother of the divine Caesar." Revelation 12 tells the real one.

Exodus again

The woman is given "the two wings of the great eagle" to fly into the wilderness (12:14), quoting God's words at Sinai: "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles" (Exodus 19:4). She is fed there (12:6), as Israel was fed with manna. The earth opens its mouth and swallows the flood (12:16), as it swallowed Pharaoh's army (Exodus 15:12) and Korah's rebels (Numbers 16:32).
The chapter states its time period two ways: 1,260 days (12:6) and "a time, and times, and half a time" (12:14). Both describe the same stay in the wilderness, so the two phrases name one period.

deep.title: Leto, Python and the newborn god
deep.b: In the Greek story the dragon Python hunts the pregnant goddess Leto to kill her child. She is carried to safety, gives birth to Apollo, and Apollo later kills the dragon (Hyginus, Fabulae 140). Ephesus claimed that Leto gave birth in a grove near the city (Tacitus, Annals 3.61), so John's first readers knew the tale. Many scholars think Revelation 12 retells it on purpose: the true child who defeats the dragon is Jesus, not Apollo, the god the emperors claimed (Adela Yarbro Collins, The Combat Myth in the Book of Revelation, 1976).

deep.title: The god who defeats the sea dragon
deep.note: shared imagery, used by the Old Testament
deep.b: Across the ancient Near East, a god defeats a sea monster to bring order to the world. In the Enuma Elish, Marduk splits the sea-dragon Tiamat in two. At Ugarit, Baal crushes Yam, the Sea. The Old Testament borrows this picture for the true God (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 51:9). Revelation completes it: the dragon is thrown down, and in the end the sea itself is gone (21:1).

deep.title: Isis hides Horus from Set
deep.b: Egyptian myth tells how the goddess Isis hid her infant son Horus in the marshes of the Nile Delta to protect him from his murderous uncle Set, who later took the form of beasts. A mother hiding her child from a monster in a wild place is an old and widespread story shape.

deep.title: Revelation’s only "rapture" is the ascension of Jesus
deep.b: The verb Paul uses for believers being "caught up" (1 Thessalonians 4:17) appears once in Revelation: for the child in 12:5. In Revelation's story, the Son's being caught up to the throne is the event that throws the dragon out of heaven (12:7–10). My speculation: Revelation reframes the rapture question. The church's hope is pictured as following the Lamb's own path, "wherever he goes" (14:4): faithful witness, death, resurrection, then "Come up here," exactly the sequence of the two witnesses (11:7–12). If that is right, the book does not ask "will we escape before the trouble?" but "will we follow where he went?" This lands closest to post-tribulation and idealist readings, and it is my own synthesis.

echoes: Genesis 3:15; Genesis 37:9; Isaiah 66:7–8; Isaiah 26:17–18; Micah 4:10; Psalm 2:9; Daniel 7:25; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 12:1; Exodus 19:4; Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1; Job 1:6–12; Zechariah 3:1; Luke 10:18; John 12:31

settings.what: The victory song after the war in heaven
settings.by: a loud voice in heaven
settings.to: the heavens, and a warning to the earth and the sea; heard by John
settings.when: after Michael throws the dragon down
settings.why: The song explains the churches' suffering. Satan has lost in heaven and rages on earth because he knows "he has only a little time." The believers win the victory over him "because of the blood of the Lamb" and because of their testimony, even if it costs their lives. Persecution is a sign of the dragon's defeat, not of his strength.

traditions.q: Is the woman dressed in the sun, who gives birth to the Messiah (12:1–6), Mary?
views: Yes, and also the people of God. The Church reads 11:19 and 12:1–6 on the feast of the Assumption: the ark of the covenant seen in heaven is followed by the woman, and Mary is the ark who carried Christ. Pius XII noted that teachers of the church saw Mary's glory in this woman (Munificentissimus Deus 27), and the Catechism names Mary as the Woman in heaven's worship (Catechism 1138).

Mainly the church. Andrew of Caesarea, the standard Orthodox commentator, reports that some understand her as the Mother of God but follows Methodius in seeing the church, which always gives birth to Christ in believers. The Marian reading is honored, not required.

The faithful people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah was born, continuing as the church that the dragon still attacks (12:17). Some Protestants allow that Mary is in the background, as the mother of the child, but not that the chapter teaches about her.

National Israel. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph's dream of his family (Genesis 37:9), and the woman's flight into the wilderness is Israel protected in the last three and a half years of the tribulation.

title: The Two Beasts
sum: The dragon stands on the seashore. A beast rises from the sea with ten crowned horns and seven heads. It looks like a leopard with a bear's feet and a lion's mouth. One head looks slaughtered, but its death wound is healed, and the whole earth worships: "Who is like the beast? Who is able to fight it?" It acts for 42 months and makes war on the saints.

A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb's, but it talks like a dragon. It works signs, sets up a talking image of the first beast, and forces everyone to take a mark on the right hand or forehead to buy or sell. "Its number is 666."

readings: Read literally
A future world ruler, the Antichrist, with a global government; a false prophet with real miracles; a literal mark required to buy and sell.
Read as symbol

The sea beast mixes all four of Daniel's beasts into one: every empire rolled together, first of all Rome. The land beast is the religion and propaganda that serve it. The mark copies God's seal (7:3) and the Shema's command to tie God's words "as a sign on your hand" and as "a band between your eyes" (Deuteronomy 6:8).

views.P: The beast is Nero; "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters adds up to 666. The healed wound is Rome nearly collapsing in AD 69 and then recovering.
views.H: The Reformers' reading: the sea beast is the papacy, and 42 months are 1,260 years.
views.F: A future Antichrist and false prophet, ruling for the second half of Daniel's seventieth "week" (Daniel 9:27).
views.I: Every age has its beasts: political power that wants worship, and the voices that make people give it.

deep.b:
Daniel’s four beasts in one

Daniel 7Revelation 13:1–2
1. A lion with eagle’s wings (Babylon)"A mouth like a lion"
2. A bear (Media and Persia)"Feet like a bear"
3. A leopard with four heads (Greece)"Like a leopard"
4. A terrible beast with ten horns (usually Rome)Ten horns, seven heads

Daniel’s four beasts have seven heads in all (1 + 1 + 4 + 1). John’s beast has all seven, and he lists the animals in reverse order, looking back from his own day: every empire before rolled into one.

The image that speaks

The land beast makes an image of the sea beast "speak" (13:15). Ancient temples were known for statues that seemed to move or speak. The satirist Lucian describes Alexander of Abonoteichus, a false prophet in Asia Minor around AD 150, whose snake-god Glycon had a linen head that "spoke" through a hidden tube (Alexander the False Prophet 26). Calling fire down from heaven (13:13) imitates Elijah (1 Kings 18:38). False prophecy works by copying true signs.

"Who is like the beast?"

The world's question (13:4) copies Israel's song at the sea: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11). It is also a play on the name Michael, which means "Who is like God?" In chapter 12 Michael wins; in chapter 13 the world asks the wrong question.

The beast's healed head is described with the same words as the Lamb: ὡς ἐσφαγμένην, "as slaughtered" (13:3; compare 5:6). The dragon, the beast and the false prophet copy the Father, the Son and the Spirit. Scholars call them the unholy trinity.

After Nero killed himself in AD 68, rumors spread that he was not really dead and would return from the east with a Parthian army. At least three men later claimed to be Nero (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57). Scholars call this the Nero redivivus ("Nero alive again") legend.

The Hebrew spelling "Neron Qesar" (נרון קסר), the one that adds up to 666, is found in an Aramaic document from Wadi Murabba'at near the Dead Sea, dated to Nero's reign. And 666 is a "triangular" number: 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 36 = 666.

deep.title: Litan, the serpent with seven heads
deep.b: Clay tablets from Ugarit, about 1300 BC, describe Litan (Lotan), "the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads," defeated by Baal. Isaiah 27:1 uses almost the same words for Leviathan. Seven-headed monsters also appear on Mesopotamian cylinder seals. When John describes a seven-headed beast, he is using a picture of chaos that was already 1,400 years old.

deep.title: Al-Masih ad-Dajjal, the false messiah
deep.b: In Islamic tradition, the Dajjal ("the deceiver") appears before the end, works false miracles, claims to be divine and leads many astray, until Jesus returns and kills him. The hadith say the word kafir ("unbeliever") is written between his eyes, so the faithful can read it (Sahih Muslim). Here the mark is on the deceiver's own forehead. These traditions were written down centuries after Revelation.

deep.title: 666 and the king who broke the king’s law
deep.b: The number 666 appears in one other place: the gold that came to Solomon in one year, 666 talents (1 Kings 10:14). That link is well known. What I rarely see noticed is the rest of the chapter. It goes on to list exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbade Israel's king to pile up: gold, horses from Egypt, and (in chapter 11) many wives. It also describes Solomon controlling the horse and chariot trade (1 Kings 10:28–29). Revelation 13:17 is about controlling who can buy and sell. My speculation: "the number of a man" points to the moment a king of God's own people turned into a Pharaoh. The beast is not only a pagan threat from outside. It is what God's people become when they grasp at wealth, weapons and control.

echoes: Daniel 7:1–8; Daniel 7:21; Daniel 7:25; Daniel 3:1–7; Jeremiah 15:2; Jeremiah 43:11; Deuteronomy 6:8; Deuteronomy 13:1–3; 1 Kings 10:14; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–10

settings.what: "Whoever has ears should listen"
settings.by: John, breaking into the vision
settings.to: the churches hearing the book read
settings.when: after the beast from the sea makes war on God's people
settings.why: John uses the same words that end each of the seven letters, so the hearers know this is meant for them. The saying, based on Jeremiah 15:2, tells them not to fight back but to accept captivity or death if it comes. "This is where the saints show their endurance and their faith."
views: Manuscripts differ in 13:10 (see the two variants). In the Byzantine text and the KJV, whoever kills with the sword must be killed with the sword, a warning against taking up arms, like Matthew 26:52. In the oldest form, kept by the critical editions, the saying is about accepting what comes.

settings.what: The mark and the riddle of 666
settings.by: John
settings.to: the churches, "whoever has understanding"
settings.when: after the beast from the earth makes everyone take the mark
settings.why: "Nobody can buy or sell" unless they have the mark. For hearers in trading cities, the picture of the economy bound up with worship of the beast was close to home. John then gives a puzzle meant to be solved: "it is a human number." In the ancient practice of gematria, letters stood for numbers. A few manuscripts read 616, which also fits the name Nero Caesar spelled in Hebrew in its Latin form.
views: Preterists, and many late-date scholars too, read 666 as Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters, perhaps as the Nero expected to return.
Futurists expect a coming Antichrist whose name will fit the number.

Historicists read it as the papacy, often through the Greek word Lateinos, "the Latin one," whose letters add up to 666, one of the names Irenaeus already suggested (he himself preferred Teitan, and the papacy as later known did not yet exist).
Idealists read it as the number of imperfection: six, short of seven, three times over.

traditions.q: Is the beast of chapter 13, or the Antichrist, the papacy?
views: Historically, yes. Luther's Smalcald Articles say the pope is the very Antichrist, and his 1530 preface reads the second beast of chapter 13 as the papacy, which set up a new Roman Empire as the beast's image. The Missouri Synod's Brief Statement (1932) still says this, though many Lutherans, especially those in dialogue with Rome, no longer do.

Historically, yes. The Westminster Confession of 1646 (and the 1689 Baptist confession) called the pope "that Antichrist." Many Presbyterian churches have since removed the line, and most Reformed scholars now read the beast as Rome in John's day and the powers like it.

Yes. Traditional Adventist teaching, following Ellen White, reads the sea beast as papal Rome, the 42 months as 1,260 years (AD 538–1798), and the healing of its wound as the papacy's return to power; the land beast is the United States, which will one day enforce worship on Sunday.

No. The beast is the emperor-worshiping Rome that killed Peter and Paul and the martyrs, and every power that demands worship. The Antichrist is a final religious lie in which people put themselves in the place of God (Catechism 675–676).

No. Following Irenaeus, Hippolytus and Andrew of Caesarea, the Orthodox expect the Antichrist to be a single deceiver near the end of history, and see beasts at work wherever the state claims worship.
No. The beast is a future world ruler at the head of a revived Roman Empire, who makes and then breaks a treaty with Israel (Daniel 9:27) and rules for the last three and a half years.

title: The Lamb on Mount Zion
sum: Right after the beasts, a contrast. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who carry his name and his Father's name on their foreheads instead of the beast's mark. They "follow the Lamb wherever he goes."

Three angels fly overhead: one with "eternal good news" for every nation, one announcing "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great," and one warning those who take the beast's mark. Then come two harvests: one like a son of man reaps the earth with a sickle, and an angel gathers grapes into the winepress of God's anger.

readings: Read literally
The 144,000 stand with Christ on the real Mount Zion. The bloodshed is a real battle near Jerusalem; some note that 1,600 stadia is roughly the length of the land of Israel.
Read as symbol

1,600 is 4 × 4 × 100, the four corners of the earth squared: judgment that covers the world. The grain harvest is often the gathering of God's people (Matthew 13:30), while grapes and the winepress mean judgment (Isaiah 63:1–6; Joel 3:13).

views.P: The harvest of Judea in AD 70.
views.H: The three angels picture later movements of world mission and reform. Seventh-day Adventists see the three angels' messages as their own calling.
views.F: Events just before Christ returns, in order.
views.I: The gospel goes out, empire falls, and history ends in a harvest.

deep.b:
Three angels, two harvests

VersesWhat happensMeaning
14:6–7First angel: "eternal good news" for every nation: fear God, worship the CreatorA last call to repent
14:8Second angel: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great"From Isaiah 21:9; told ahead of chapter 18
14:9–11Third angel: those who take the mark drink God’s wineThe cost of worshiping the beast
14:12–13"Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord"The second of seven blessings
14:14–16One like a son of man reaps the grain with a sickleUsually the gathering of God’s people
14:17–20An angel gathers grapes into the winepress of God’s angerJudgment; from Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1–6

Blood to the horses’ bridles

The winepress is trodden "outside the city," and blood flows "up to the horses' bridles, for 1,600 stadia" (14:20), about 184 miles. 1 Enoch describes a final judgment in which "A horse will wade up to its chest in the blood of sinners" (1 Enoch 100:3), and later rabbinic tradition used similar words for Bar Kokhba's last stand at Betar in AD 135. 1,600 is 40 × 40, or 4 × 4 × 100: the four corners of the earth, squared and multiplied. Jesus too suffered "outside the city gate" (Hebrews 13:12).

Firstfruits

The 144,000 are "firstfruits to God and to the Lamb" (14:4). In Israel the first sheaf of the harvest was given to God as a promise that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10). If the 144,000 are firstfruits, a larger harvest is still coming, which is exactly what 14:14–16 shows.

echoes: Psalm 2:6; Joel 2:32; Jeremiah 2:3; Isaiah 21:9; Daniel 4:30; Jeremiah 51:7; Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15; Isaiah 51:17; Genesis 19:24; Isaiah 34:9–10; Daniel 7:13; Joel 3:13; Isaiah 63:1–6

settings.what: The new song before the throne, learned by the 144,000
settings.by: a choir in heaven, like harpists (some say the 144,000 themselves)
settings.to: sung before the throne, the creatures and the elders; heard by John
settings.when: right after the visions of the two beasts and the mark
settings.why: In contrast to those who take the beast's mark, the 144,000 carry the Lamb's name. They alone can learn heaven's new song, and they "follow the Lamb wherever he goes." For the churches, the picture shows what faithfulness looks like. Some read the group as an army kept ready for holy war, and their purity as refusing the idolatry Revelation calls sexual sin.
views: Many futurists read them as ethnic Israel or Jewish believers. Bauckham, Beale and others read them as the whole church, pictured as the true Israel. Others read them as the martyrs.
Most read the words about women as a picture of refusing idolatry. Some read a holy-war rule, as soldiers kept apart before battle. A few read literal celibacy.

settings.what: The messages of the three angels
settings.by: three angels, a voice from heaven and the Spirit
settings.to: "those who live on the earth," every nation, and through John the churches
settings.when: before the harvest of the earth and the bowls
settings.why: The first angel calls all nations to "Fear God and give him glory" and to worship the Creator: a last call to repent. The second announces Babylon's fall ahead of time. The third warns that anyone who worships the beast and takes its mark will share God's anger. For believers tempted to join the club feasts and honor the emperor to keep their business and standing, the warning is meant to make the cost of compromise plain. Then come comfort and a call: "This is where the saints show their endurance," and a blessing on those who die in the Lord.
views: Preterists and many others link the mark to taking part in emperor worship and the trade and civic life bound up with it. Historicists read it as loyalty to papal Rome. Futurists often expect a future mark. Idealists read it as any loyalty to a power that takes God's place.

settings.what: The two harvests: the angels' calls to reap
settings.by: an angel from the temple, and an angel from the altar who has authority over the fire
settings.to: the one like a son of man on the cloud, and an angel with a sickle; heard by John
settings.when: after the three angels' messages, before the bowls
settings.why: Two calls, "Put in your sickle," start two harvests. The first is grain, reaped by the one like a son of man; the second is grapes, thrown into the winepress of God's anger. The calls come from the temple and from the altar, the place where the martyrs' prayers rose (6:9–10; 8:3–5), so the harvest is God's answer to them. For churches under pressure, it says the time of the harvest is set by God, not by Rome.
views: Many read the grain as the gathering of believers (Matthew 13:30; Mark 4:29) and the grapes as judgment (Joel 3:13; Isaiah 63:1–6). Others read both as judgment, as Joel 3:13 pairs the sickle and the winepress.
Most see Christ in the one like a son of man (1:13; Daniel 7:13); some see an angel, since he takes the order to reap from an angel.

title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
sum: The shortest chapter in Revelation. Seven angels appear with the seven last plagues. At a sea of glass mixed with fire stand those who won the victory over the beast. They hold harps of God and sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb.

The temple in heaven, "the tent of the testimony," opens. One of the living creatures hands the angels seven gold bowls full of God's anger, and the temple fills with smoke so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished.

readings: Read literally
A real heavenly temple, from which the final judgments come.
Read as symbol

The sea of glass is the Red Sea, crossed. Israel sang the song of Moses on the far shore after Pharaoh's army drowned (Exodus 15). Now God's people stand on the far side of the beast. The song itself quotes Psalms and Jeremiah and never mentions the people's own victory, only God's.

views.P: The final stage of judgment on Jerusalem prepared in heaven.
views.H: The prelude to the bowls, which some read as the French Revolution and the decline of papal power.
views.F: The prelude to the last and worst judgments at the very end of the tribulation.
views.I: God's people already stand on the far shore, singing, even while judgment falls.

deep.b:
What the song of Moses and the Lamb quotes

Line in 15:3–4Source
"Great and amazing are your works"Psalm 111:2; Psalm 139:14
"Lord God, the Almighty"Amos 4:13 (in the Greek Old Testament)
"Your ways are just and true"Deuteronomy 32:4 (the other song of Moses)
"King of the nations ... who will not fear you"Jeremiah 10:7
"All the nations will come and worship in front of you"Psalm 86:9
"Your acts of justice have been made plain"Psalm 98:2

Not one line comes from the song Moses sang at the Red Sea (Exodus 15). That song celebrated enemies drowned; this one celebrates the nations coming to worship (Richard Bauckham, The Climax of Prophecy).

A sea mixed with fire

The victors stand beside "a sea of glass mixed with fire" (15:2), the sea before the throne (4:6), now like the Red Sea with Pharaoh's army behind it. Like Israel on the far shore, they sing. Then the temple fills with smoke "from the glory of God" and no one can enter (15:8), as when the cloud filled the tabernacle and Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:34–35) and when Isaiah saw the temple fill with smoke (Isaiah 6:4).

echoes: Exodus 15:1–18; Deuteronomy 32; Psalm 86:9; Jeremiah 10:7; Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11

settings.what: The song of Moses and the Lamb
settings.by: those who won the victory over the beast
settings.to: God, the "King of the nations"
settings.when: beside the sea of glass, before the seven bowls
settings.why: As Israel sang beside the sea after the Exodus, the faithful sing after their own rescue. The words come almost entirely from the psalms and prophets. The song does not praise their own victory but God's justice, and it hopes that "All the nations will come and worship." Even before the last plagues, the goal is the nations turning to God.

title: Seven Bowls and Armageddon
sum: The bowls pour out on the earth (painful sores on those with the mark), the sea and the rivers (turned to blood), the sun (scorching heat), the beast's throne (darkness), and the Euphrates, which dries up for "the kings from where the sun rises." Three unclean spirits like frogs go out to the kings of the world, and the kings are brought together "to the place called in Hebrew Armageddon."

The seventh bowl: "It is done!" The greatest earthquake ever splits the great city in three, and hailstones weighing about a talent each fall. Still people insult God. The trumpets struck a third. The bowls strike everything. The warnings are over.

readings: Read literally
A final world war gathering in the Jezreel Valley near Megiddo in northern Israel, and a literal drying of the Euphrates.
Read as symbol

Megiddo was a famous battlefield, so "Armageddon" stands for the final showdown between God and the powers of the world. Drying the Euphrates recalls how Cyrus diverted the river to capture Babylon, and the drying of the Red Sea and the Jordan.

views.P: The end of the Roman siege of Jerusalem; the "kings from the east" are the legions Titus brought from the Euphrates.
views.H: The sixth bowl is the slow drying up of the Ottoman Empire in the 1800s.
views.F: Future judgments at the end of the tribulation, ending in a literal campaign of Armageddon.
views.I: The last conflict of good and evil, shown in every crisis of history.

deep.b:
Bowls, trumpets and plagues side by side

TargetTrumpetBowlEgypt
LandHail and fire; a third burned (8:7)Painful sores (16:2)Boils (Exodus 9:10)
SeaA third becomes blood (8:8)All becomes blood; everything dies (16:3)Nile to blood (Exodus 7:20)
Rivers and springsA third turned bitter (8:10)Turned to blood (16:4)Nile to blood (Exodus 7:20)
SunA third darkened (8:12)Scorches people with fire (16:8)—
Throne of the beast / the abyssLocusts from the abyss; darkness (9:1–2)Darkness on the beast’s kingdom (16:10)Darkness (Exodus 10:22)
EuphratesFour angels released (9:14)Dried up for the kings from where the sun rises (16:12)—
The endThe kingdom of the world passes to our Lord and his Messiah (11:15)"It is done!" (16:17)—

The trumpets hit a third; the bowls hit everything. The pattern is the main evidence for reading the two series as the same judgments told twice, the second time in full.

How Babylon fell the first time

The Greek historian Herodotus says Cyrus captured Babylon in 539 BC by diverting the Euphrates and marching his army in along the dry riverbed (Histories 1.191). The prophets had said God would dry up Babylon's waters (Isaiah 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; Jeremiah 51:36). When the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates for "the kings from where the sun rises" (16:12), it replays the night Babylon fell, and points to Rome's own fear of the Parthians beyond that river.

Hail as heavy as a talent

The last plague is hail, each stone "about a talent in weight" (16:21), very roughly 60 to 90 pounds (the talent varied by region). It echoes the seventh Egyptian plague (Exodus 9:24) and the hailstones God threw down on the Canaanite kings (Joshua 10:11). Like Pharaoh, the people harden themselves; worse, they insult God (16:9, 11, 21).

Tel Megiddo holds the ruins of more than 20 cities built one on top of another over about 4,000 years. It guarded the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, which is why so many armies fought there. Pharaoh Thutmose III's battle there, around 1457 BC, is the first battle in history recorded in detail.

deep.title: Frogs: the last trick the magicians could copy
deep.b: The bowls follow the plagues of Egypt closely: sores, blood, darkness, frogs, hail. The frogs are a curious detail. In Exodus, frogs were the last plague Pharaoh's magicians could copy (Exodus 8:7). At the next plague, gnats, they failed and said, "It is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19; compare Exodus 8:18). In Revelation 16:13 the frogs come out of the mouths of the false prophet and his allies, the ones who do counterfeit signs (13:13–14). My speculation: the frogs mark the last moment the counterfeit still works. Right after them comes "It is done," and every imitation of God's power stops at once. I have not seen the Exodus 8 detail used this way.

echoes: Exodus 9:9–11; Exodus 7:17–21; Exodus 10:21; Exodus 8:2–7; Exodus 9:23–24; Judges 5:19; 2 Kings 23:29; Zechariah 12:11; Isaiah 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; Jeremiah 51:36; Daniel 12:1; John 19:30

settings.what: The voice from the temple: "Go!" and "It is done!"
settings.by: a loud voice from the temple, from the throne (God himself, most readers say, since the temple is closed to all, 15:8)
settings.to: the seven angels with the bowls (16:1); then the whole creation (16:17); heard by John
settings.when: 16:1 sends the seven angels out; 16:17 speaks as the seventh bowl is poured into the air
settings.why: The same voice opens and closes the bowls. "Go! Pour out" puts every plague under God's command, not the beast's; "It is done!" says the judgments have reached their end, and 21:6 repeats it over the new creation. For churches that felt Rome's power had no end, the two words set a limit on it.

settings.what: The angel's praise of God's justice
settings.by: the angel of the waters, and the altar
settings.to: God
settings.when: after the third bowl turns the rivers to blood
settings.why: The short song answers the martyrs' cry in 6:10. Those who shed the blood of God's people are given blood to drink. For churches that knew of Antipas's death and feared more deaths, it says God's judgments are true and just.

settings.what: Jesus breaks in: "I am coming like a thief"
settings.by: Jesus
settings.to: the churches hearing the book
settings.when: in the middle of the sixth bowl, as the kings gather for Armageddon
settings.why: Jesus suddenly speaks straight to the hearers with the third of the book's seven blessings. The words echo the letters to Sardis, where Jesus warns he will come like a thief (3:3), and Laodicea, where he offers white clothes to cover the shame of their nakedness (3:18). Even in the great battle scene, the point for the churches is to stay awake and faithful now.

title: The Woman on the Scarlet Beast
sum: An angel shows John "the great prostitute who sits on many waters." She rides a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. She wears purple and scarlet, gold, jewels and pearls, holds a gold cup full of filth, and is drunk with the blood of the saints. Her forehead reads: "Babylon the Great, the mother of prostitutes."

The angel explains. The seven heads are seven mountains, and also seven kings: five have fallen, one is, one is still to come. The ten horns are ten kings who give their power to the beast, then turn on the woman and burn her. "The woman you saw is the great city that holds royal power over the kings of the earth."

readings: Read literally
A real future city and system: a rebuilt Babylon in Iraq, Rome, Jerusalem, or a world trade center, together with a one-world false religion that the Antichrist uses and then destroys.
Read as symbol

Early Christians used "Babylon" as a code name for Rome (1 Peter 5:13). Rome sat on seven hills, was the world's great port city, and ruled over kings. The prostitute is the seductive side of empire: money, luxury and false worship. She is the opposite of the Bride of chapters 19–21.

views.P: Either Rome (seven hills, emperors as heads) or Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful bride, as in Ezekiel 16.
views.H: Papal Rome, in the Reformers' reading.
views.F: A future Babylon, as a city or a global system, plus an end-time false religion.
views.I: The world system of greed and false worship in every age, which will surely fall.

deep.b:
Counting the seven kings (17:10)

Start withCount"One is" (the sixth)"Not yet come" (the seventh)The eighth
Julius CaesarEvery rulerNero (54–68)Galba, who reigned 7 monthsA Nero-like figure
AugustusEvery rulerGalba (68–69)Otho, 3 monthsVitellius or Vespasian
AugustusSkip the three short reigns of 68–69Vespasian (69–79)Titus, 2 yearsDomitian, whom the poet Juvenal called "a bald Nero" (Satires 4.38)
—Seven world empires: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome, and one to comeRomeA future empireThe final beast
—Seven as a symbol of completenessThe present evil powerIts brief final formEvil’s last return

Each way of counting supports a different date for the book. The angel’s warning, "Here a mind that has wisdom is needed" (17:9), suggests the first readers were meant to work it out.

The city on seven hills

Rome was famous as the city of seven hills: the poets Virgil (Georgics 2.535), Horace (Secular Hymn 7) and Martial all called it that, and a yearly festival, the Septimontium, celebrated them. Many first-century readers would have taken "seven mountains, and the woman sits on them" (17:9) as Rome. Those who identify Babylon with Jerusalem note that Jerusalem too was described as set among hills, but "seven hills" was Rome's nickname.

The beast turns on the woman

In 17:16 the beast and its ten horns hate the prostitute, lay her waste, leave her naked, eat her flesh and burn her. Evil destroys itself: the power that carried the city in the end devours it. Ezekiel pictured Jerusalem's lovers turning on her in just this way (Ezekiel 23:25–29). Preterists see the Roman armies burning Jerusalem, or Rome burning in AD 64 or 69; others see any system that consumes those who rely on it.

A Roman coin minted under Emperor Vespasian in AD 71 shows the goddess Roma sitting on seven hills, with the river Tiber beside her. Several scholars think John's first readers could have seen Revelation 17 as a dark parody of that very image.

echoes: Jeremiah 51:7, 13; Ezekiel 16:15–41; Daniel 7:7, 24; Isaiah 23:17; Nahum 3:4

settings.what: The angel explains the woman and the beast
settings.by: one of the seven angels with the bowls
settings.to: John, and through him the churches
settings.when: after John is amazed at the woman on the scarlet beast
settings.why: The angel gives clues the first readers could decode: seven mountains (Rome was the city on seven hills), seven kings, and "the great city that holds royal power over the kings of the earth." The aim was to help believers see the empire's glittering capital through heaven's eyes, so that they would not admire it.
views: Most scholars read the woman as Rome and its economy and the kings as emperors, though they count the kings in different ways, which affects the date of the book.
Some preterists read the prostitute as the Jerusalem that rejected Jesus.
Historicists, including the Reformers, read Babylon and the beast as papal Rome.
A future power or every empire
Futurists often expect a revived Rome or a world system to come; idealists see every proud, wealthy power.

traditions.q: Who is Babylon the prostitute (chapters 17–18), and what does "Come out of her, my people" (18:4) ask?
views: Pagan imperial Rome, the city on seven hills that killed the martyrs, which 1 Peter 5:13 already calls Babylon; and every worldly power like it. Some Catholic writers, such as Scott Hahn, read her instead as Jerusalem that had become unfaithful.

Babylon is the kingdom of this world set against God. Andrew of Caesarea, the classic Greek commentator on Revelation, reads her as worldly power, in John's day pagan Rome, and at the end the seat of the Antichrist's kingdom. The Orthodox Church does not use the chapter against other churches, and Revelation is not read in its public services.

Luther's prefaces to Revelation read the beast and Babylon as the papacy, and the Lutheran confessions call the papacy the Antichrist (Smalcald Articles II.4; Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope). Many Lutherans today read Babylon more broadly, as every worldly power that persecutes the church, while the confessions still stand.

The Reformers read Babylon as papal Rome: the Geneva Bible's notes say so plainly (at 17:5 and 17:9). Most Reformed scholars today read first-century Rome and, behind it, every society built on idolatry and greed.

Babylon is fallen religion: Rome and the churches that keep her teachings, such as Sunday worship. "Come out of her" is God's last call to his true people, many of whom are still in those churches, to leave before the end.

A future false world religion (chapter 17) and a future world economy or city (chapter 18), which some think will be Babylon in Iraq rebuilt. The beast will turn on the religious system before God judges both.

title: Babylon Falls
sum: An angel lights the earth with his glory and shouts, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great!" A voice calls, "Come out of her, my people." Then comes a funeral song. Kings, merchants and sailors stand far away and weep, not for the city, but for their lost trade. The long cargo list ends with "bodies, and human souls," the traders' word for slaves and John's reminder of what they are.

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon will be thrown down. Music, work, lamplight and weddings will never be heard in her again. Heaven is told to celebrate, because God has judged her for the blood of his people.

Who is Babylon? The answer shapes how you read chapters 14 and 16–19. Below the four views are her names in the Greek, the real Babylon and where it was, the main identifications through history (including when Jerusalem and the church have been called "Babylon"), and what her symbols mean.

readings: Read literally
The sudden destruction of a real city, "in one hour," perhaps by fire.
Read as symbol

The chapter is woven from the prophets' songs over Babylon (Jeremiah 50–51; Isaiah 47) and Tyre (Ezekiel 26–27). It is a warning about wealth and trade built on people. "Come out of her" is a call to live differently inside the empire, not necessarily to move.

views.P: Rome's fall, or Jerusalem's burning in AD 70.
views.H: The final fall of papal Rome.
views.F: The future destruction of the end-time Babylon.
views.I: Every economy built on luxury and exploitation is already under this sentence.

deep.b:
Babylon’s names in Revelation

Revelation uses "Babylon" by name six times (14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2; 18:10; 18:21). It also gives her a cluster of other names and titles, each with its own source:

  • Babylon the GreatBabylōn hē megalē (14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2). From Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Daniel 4:30, which in the Aramaic runs: "Isn't this great Babylon, which I built myself as a royal home, by my own great strength and for the honor of my splendor?" The name itself carries pride.
  • The great cityhē polis hē megalē (16:19; 17:18; 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21). Also used in 11:8 for the city "where their Lord too was crucified," which is why some read Babylon as Jerusalem.
  • The mighty cityhē polis hē ischyra (18:10). Strength is her claim; she falls "in one hour."
  • The great prostitutehē pornē hē megalē (17:1; 19:2). The prophets' word for idolatry as unfaithfulness, and also for trade sold to anyone (Isaiah 23:15–18 of Tyre).
  • Mother of prostitutes"and of the disgusting things of the earth" (17:5). She is the source of many smaller copies.
  • A mysterymystērion (17:5, 7). Her name is a secret to be decoded, a sign it is not meant literally.
  • The womanhē gynē (17:3–18), set against the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the bride (19:7; 21:9).
  • A queen"I sit as a queen. I am no widow" (18:7), from Isaiah 47:7–8.
  • She who sits on many waters(17:1), from Jeremiah 51:13. Explained in 17:15 as "peoples, crowds, nations, and languages."

Revelation also says the great city is called Sodom and Egypt "symbolically" (pneumatikōs, literally "spiritually," 11:8). The book itself tells you these city names are spiritual labels.

The real Babylon

Babylon stood on the Euphrates in what is now Iraq, near the modern town of Hillah. In Hebrew it is Bavel, the same word as Babel in Genesis 11. Its own people called it Bāb-ili, "gate of the god." Genesis puns on it with bālal, "confuse" (Genesis 11:9).

  • About 1750 BC: King Hammurabi makes Babylon a great power and issues his famous law code.
  • 605–562 BC: Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilds the city in glory: the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, the great ziggurat Etemenanki (often linked to the Tower of Babel), and, by tradition, the Hanging Gardens.
  • 586 BC: his army burns Jerusalem and Solomon's temple and takes the people into exile (2 Kings 25). Psalm 137: "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept."
  • 539 BC: the city falls to Cyrus of Persia in a single night (Daniel 5), and the exiles may go home (Ezra 1).
  • After 300 BC: the Seleucid kings build a new capital nearby, and Babylon slowly empties. By John's day it was mostly ruins. The geographer Strabo, quoting a poet, said "the great city is a great desert" (Geography 16.1.5).
  • Today: Saddam Hussein rebuilt parts of the palace in the 1980s, stamping bricks with his name like Nebuchadnezzar. The ruins became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

So when Revelation was written, Babylon on the Euphrates was not a world power. John's readers would have heard the name the way we might hear "Waterloo" or "Pharaoh": a famous past standing for something present.

Place, symbol, or ideal?

All three, depending on the reader. The main identifications:

Rome

The view of most scholars, ancient and modern. She sits on seven hills (17:9), holds royal power "over the kings of the earth" (17:18), and grows rich by sea trade (18:17–19). After Rome destroyed the second temple in AD 70, Jewish and Christian writers called Rome "Babylon," because it had done what Babylon did (1 Peter 5:13; 4 Ezra 3:1–2, 28; 2 Baruch 11:1; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159).

Jerusalem

Held by many preterists (e.g. Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton). "The great city" is "where their Lord too was crucified" (11:8); "in her was found the blood of prophets" (18:24) echoes Jesus's words to Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35–37); and the prophets often called Jerusalem a prostitute (see below).

A rebuilt city on the Euphrates

Some futurists expect a literal Babylon to rise again in Iraq, since Isaiah 13:19–20 and Jeremiah 50–51 say it will be destroyed and never inhabited again. Charles Dyer's The Rise of Babylon (1991) made this popular during Saddam's rebuilding.

Papal Rome

The standard Protestant reading from the Reformation to the 1800s (see "Has the church been called Babylon?" below).

Other modern guesses

Writers have named New York, the United States, Mecca, the European Union and the United Nations. None has a clear basis in the text, and each was shaped by its own era's headlines.

A system, in every age

The idealist reading: Babylon is human society organized against God, around power, luxury and false worship. Augustine called it "the earthly city," which "loves itself even to the contempt of God" (City of God 14.28). Every age has a Babylon, and the church always lives in it.

These can overlap. Many readers think John meant Rome for his first readers, and that Rome stands for every power that acts like it.

Was Israel ever called Babylon?

Not in so many words. No book of the Bible calls Jerusalem or Israel "Babylon." But the prophets came close, and in ways that matter for Revelation 17–18:

  • Jerusalem is called Sodom (Isaiah 1:10; Ezekiel 16:46–49), and Revelation 11:8 calls "the great city" "Sodom and Egypt."
  • Jerusalem is called a prostitute: "How has she turned into a prostitute, the town that was faithful!" (Isaiah 1:21; also Jeremiah 3:1–3; Hosea 2; Ezekiel 16 and 23).
  • Ezekiel 16 dresses unfaithful Jerusalem in fine linen, embroidered cloth, gold and jewels (16:10–13), and then her own lovers strip her and burn her houses (16:37–41). Revelation 17:16 has the beast and the ten horns do the same to the prostitute.

Preterists who read Babylon as Jerusalem lean on these parallels. Others answer that Revelation borrows its words for Babylon mostly from the prophets' songs over Babylon and Tyre (Jeremiah 50–51; Isaiah 47; Ezekiel 26–27), not from the oracles against Jerusalem, and that Jerusalem in AD 70 did not hold royal power "over the kings of the earth" (17:18).

In later Jewish writing, Rome was the one called "Babylon" and "Edom," never Jerusalem. A caution: reading Babylon as Jerusalem has been misused to justify hostility toward Jewish people. The careful preterists who hold it apply it to first-century temple leaders, not to Jews.

Has the church been called Babylon?

In the New Testament, the church is "in" Babylon, not Babylon itself. 1 Peter 5:13: "She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings." "She" is the church in Rome, greeting other churches from the capital.

Later, yes, often, and usually by one group of Christians about another:

  • Medieval reformers. Followers of Joachim of Fiore and the Spiritual Franciscans (Peter John Olivi, about 1297) called the corrupt, worldly church "the carnal church" and "Babylon." Dante shows the harlot of Revelation 17 seated on the church's chariot (Purgatory 32).
  • The Avignon papacy (1309–1377). When the popes lived in France, Petrarch called papal Avignon "Babylon," and the period is still known as the "Babylonian captivity" of the papacy.
  • The Reformation. Martin Luther's On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520) said the papacy held the sacraments captive. The Geneva Bible's notes (1560) and many Puritans identified the papacy with the beast and Babylon, and the Westminster Confession (1646) called the pope "that Antichrist." Catholic writers such as Robert Bellarmine answered that Babylon was pagan Rome.
  • Revival movements. In 1843 the Millerite preacher Charles Fitch preached "Come Out of Her, My People," applying 18:4 to the Protestant churches that rejected the Advent message. Seventh-day Adventists still read fallen Babylon (14:8) as apostate Christianity. Jehovah's Witnesses teach that "Babylon the Great" is the world empire of false religion, Christendom included.

A pattern worth noticing: almost every group that has called another church "Babylon" has later had the label thrown back at it. Revelation itself points the warning first at its own churches: "Come out of her, my people" (18:4).

What her symbols mean

  • ProstituteSelling yourself for gain: idolatry as unfaithfulness to God, and commerce that will trade with anyone for profit (Isaiah 23:17 of Tyre).
  • Wine and the gold cup"A cup of gold, that was Babylon, in the hand of the LORD, getting the whole earth drunk" (Jeremiah 51:7). Her influence intoxicates: luxury dulls conscience.
  • Purple and scarletThe colors of wealth and rule. Tyrian purple dye was among the costliest goods in the ancient world; Roman law reserved certain purple garments for the emperor and senators.
  • Jewels and pearlsThe same stones that build the new Jerusalem (21:18–21). Babylon wears them; the bride is built from them.
  • Many watersBabylon's rivers and canals become "peoples, crowds, nations, and languages" (17:15): a power that sits on top of the nations.
  • Seven hills, seven kingsRome's geography, and its line of rulers (17:9–10).
  • Queen, not widowSelf-sufficiency and the belief that loss can never come (18:7; Isaiah 47:8). Laodicea said the same: "I am rich... I need nothing" (3:17).
  • The cargo listTwenty-eight kinds of goods by Bauckham's count (18:12–13), most of them luxury imports to Rome: silk from China, ivory from Africa, citron wood for tables that cost a fortune, cinnamon from Asia. It ends with "bodies, and human souls," the trade word for slaves and John's reminder of what they are.
  • MagicPharmakeia (18:23), a word for sorcery, spells and drugs: her deception works like a spell on the nations.
  • Smoke risingLike Sodom's smoke (Genesis 19:28). Her judgment is final.
  • The millstoneThrown like Jeremiah's scroll-stone into the Euphrates (Jeremiah 51:63–64). Ordinary life ends: no music, no crafts, no lamplight, no weddings (18:22–23).

deep.title: Jeremiah told the exiles both to settle in Babylon and to flee it
deep.b: The same prophet gave Babylon's exiles two instructions. First: "Build houses to live in... Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD. When it has peace, you will have peace" (Jeremiah 29:5–7). Later: "Come out of her, my people! Let each one save his life" (Jeremiah 51:45). Revelation quotes only the second (18:4). My reading: John's churches were meant to hold both, the way Daniel did. Daniel served Babylon's kings for decades and sought the city's good, yet would not eat the king's food or stop praying (Daniel 1:8; 6:10). Living in Babylon is not the sin. Taking part in "her sins" (18:4) is. This makes "Come out of her" a call to a different kind of life inside the city, ready to walk away when loyalty demands it, rather than a call to move somewhere else. Many commentators read 18:4 spiritually; setting it beside Jeremiah 29 and Daniel's example is my own emphasis.

echoes: Jeremiah 51:45; Jeremiah 51:63–64; Isaiah 47:7–9; Ezekiel 27:12–36; Jeremiah 25:10; Isaiah 13:21

settings.what: The angel's cry and the call to come out
settings.by: an angel with great authority, then another voice from heaven
settings.to: the world, and "my people" among the nations
settings.when: after the vision of the woman on the beast
settings.why: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great!" echoes Isaiah and Jeremiah on ancient Babylon. The voice from heaven tells God's people to leave her. Most read this as refusing to share her sins and pride. Some read a real flight, as in Jeremiah 51:45, and preterists who see Jerusalem in Babylon link it to the Christians who fled before AD 70. For merchants and workers in Asia whose living was tied to Roman trade, this was a hard and practical call.

settings.what: The laments of the kings, merchants and sailors
settings.by: the kings of the earth, the merchants, the sea traders, and then a mighty angel
settings.to: the fallen city; heard by John and the churches
settings.when: as the smoke of Babylon's burning rises
settings.why: The mourners stand far away and weep for their lost profit, not for the city. The long cargo list, from gold and silk to "bodies, and human souls," lays out the goods that flowed to Rome from across the empire, some through ports like Ephesus and Smyrna. The point for the churches is to see that economy as God sees it: built on luxury and on people bought and sold. The angel's millstone and the silence of music and lamps show it will not be rebuilt. Heaven is told to celebrate, because God has judged her for the way she treated his people.
views: Most scholars read the laments as a picture of the Roman economy in John's day, modeled on Ezekiel 27 on Tyre.

Preterists who see Babylon as Jerusalem read the laments as about the Temple's wealth. Historicists read them as the fall of papal Rome. Futurists expect a coming world economy. Idealists see the fall of every system that treats people as cargo.

title: Hallelujah and the Rider on the White Horse
sum: Heaven shouts "Hallelujah," the only place in the New Testament where the word appears. The wedding of the Lamb has come, and his bride is given fine linen, shining and clean. John falls to worship the angel and is told, "Do not do it!... Worship God!"

Heaven opens. A rider on a white horse is called Faithful and True, with eyes like fire, many crowns, and a robe dipped in blood. His name is the Word of God. The armies of heaven follow, dressed in white linen. A sharp sword comes from his mouth. The beast and the kings gather for war, but there is no description of a fight. The beast and the false prophet are captured, and the rest fall to the sword from the rider's mouth.

readings: Read literally
The visible, physical return of Jesus to earth (Acts 1:11; Zechariah 14:4), defeating real armies gathered against him.
Read as symbol

Christ wins by his word (the sword from his mouth, Isaiah 11:4) and, many think, by his own sacrifice: his robe is bloody before the battle begins. There are two suppers, the wedding supper of the Lamb and "the great supper of God" for the birds.

views.P: Many partial preterists see this as the future Second Coming; others, such as David Chilton, read it as Christ's present conquest through the gospel. Full preterists see Christ's victory through the gospel after AD 70.
views.H: The Second Coming at the end of church history.
views.F: The Second Coming at the end of the seven-year tribulation, before the thousand years.
views.I: Christ's sure victory over evil, already won at the cross.

deep.b:
The names of the rider

NameVerseEcho
Faithful and True19:11Jesus in the letter to Laodicea (3:14)
A name no one knows but he himself19:12The winners’ secret new name (2:17)
The Word of God19:13"In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1, 14)
King of kings and Lord of lords19:16; 17:14God’s title in Deuteronomy 10:17; Daniel 4:37 (Greek); 1 Timothy 6:15

Two suppers

The wedding supper of the Lamb (19:7–9)The great supper of God (19:17–18)
GuestsThose called, "blessed"The birds of the air
FoodA feast with the bridegroomThe flesh of kings, commanders and armies
SourceIsaiah 25:6–8; Matthew 22:1–14Ezekiel 39:17–20

Everyone is at a supper in chapter 19. The only question is which one.

A robe dipped in blood before the battle

The rider's robe is already "dipped in blood" (19:13) before any fighting is described. The picture comes from Isaiah 63:1–3, where God's garments are stained from treading the winepress. Many commentators (David Aune and Grant Osborne among them) take it, as in Isaiah, as the blood of his enemies. Others think of the martyrs, whose blood he now vindicates (compare the winepress of 14:20). But in Revelation the Lamb's victory was won by his own blood (5:9; 12:11), and many scholars, such as Richard Bauckham, think this is his own blood. His only weapon is the sword from his mouth (19:15, 21).

Hallelujah

"Hallelujah" is Hebrew: hallelu, "praise," and Yah, short for God's name. It opens and closes many psalms, and Psalms 113–118, the "Hallel," were sung at Passover. Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26), probably these psalms. Handel's "Hallelujah" chorus in Messiah (first performed in Dublin, 1742) sets words from 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16.

deep.title: Kalki on the white horse
deep.b: In Hindu tradition, Kalki is the tenth and last avatar of Vishnu. He comes at the end of the dark age (the Kali Yuga), riding a white horse and holding a blazing sword, to destroy evil and begin a new age of truth (Vishnu Purana; Kalki Purana). The white horse and the sword are a striking match to 19:11–15. There is no known historical link between the two.

deep.title: Saoshyant, the final savior
deep.b: Zoroastrian teaching expects a final savior, the Saoshyant, born of a virgin from the prophet's preserved seed. He leads the last battle against evil and raises the dead. Persian ideas were known in the Jewish world after the exile, and scholars still debate how much they shaped Jewish hopes about the end.

echoes: Isaiah 63:1–3; Isaiah 11:4; Psalm 2:9; Ezekiel 39:17–20; John 1:1; Matthew 22:1–14

settings.what: The Hallelujah songs, the wedding of the Lamb, and a blessing
settings.by: a huge crowd in heaven, the elders and living creatures, a voice from the throne, and the angel
settings.to: God, and the angel speaks to John
settings.when: after the fall of Babylon
settings.why: Heaven answers the laments of chapter 18 with joy. The crowd praises God for justice and announces a wedding: the church, dressed in "fine linen, shining and clean," in contrast to the prostitute's purple and gold. For the churches, the contrast is a choice between two cities and two women. The angel adds a blessing, "Blessed are those who have been called to the wedding supper of the Lamb." When John falls to worship the angel he is told "Worship God!", a sharp word for readers tempted to honor powers other than God.

settings.what: The angel's call to the birds
settings.by: an angel standing in the sun
settings.to: all the birds flying high overhead
settings.when: as the rider on the white horse goes out against the beast
settings.why: "The great supper of God" is a grim reverse of the Lamb's wedding supper (19:9), drawn from Ezekiel 39. Those who sided with the beast, from kings to slaves, end as food for birds. For the churches, the two suppers show where each loyalty leads.

title: The Thousand Years
sum: An angel binds the dragon for 1,000 years and seals him in the abyss "so that he would not lead the nations astray any longer." John sees thrones and the souls of the martyrs, who "came to life and ruled with Christ for a thousand years." John adds, "This is the first resurrection." Afterward Satan is let loose, gathers Gog and Magog against "the camp of the saints and the beloved city," and is destroyed by fire from heaven.
Then the great white throne: the dead are judged according to their deeds, and Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, "the second death." This chapter holds the biggest debate in the book.

readings: Read literally

Premillennial: Christ returns before a literal 1,000-year reign on earth, ruling from Jerusalem. Old Testament promises like the wolf living with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9) come true on this earth. Two physical resurrections are 1,000 years apart.
Read as symbol

Amillennial: the 1,000 years is the present age, from Christ's first coming to his return. Satan was "bound" at the cross so the gospel can reach the nations (Matthew 12:29). Postmillennial: the gospel slowly wins the world, bringing a long golden age before Christ returns.

views.P: Most preterists are amillennial or postmillennial: the thousand years began with Christ's first coming or after AD 70.
views.H: Historicists have held all three positions; many older Protestants were postmillennial.
views.F: Premillennial: a literal future reign on earth after the tribulation.
views.I: Amillennial: the present church age seen from heaven's side, the view of Augustine.

deep.b:
Gog and Magog, from Ezekiel to Revelation

Ezekiel 38–39Revelation 19–20
WhoGog, a ruler "of the land of Magog" (38:2)"Gog and Magog," both names for the nations (20:8)
From where"The far north" (38:15)"The four corners of the earth" (20:8)
WhenAfter Israel is restored and living in safety (38:8)After the thousand years (20:7)
Their endFire and sulfur from heaven (38:22; 39:6)Fire comes down from heaven (20:9)
AfterwardBirds feast on the fallen (39:17–20)Birds feast on the fallen (19:17–21)

Revelation uses Ezekiel 38–39 twice: the bird feast in chapter 19 and the fire from heaven in chapter 20. Amillennial writers take that as a sign that 19:17–21 and 20:7–10 are the same final battle told twice; premillennial writers see two battles a thousand years apart.

Bound, sealed, released

An angel with a key and a great chain seizes the dragon, throws him into the abyss and seals it (20:1–3). The picture recalls the fallen angels bound "in darkness" until judgment (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4) and 1 Enoch, where the angel Raphael binds the rebel Azazel and throws him into a pit in the desert (1 Enoch 10:4–6). Jesus said he had bound "the strong man" so he could plunder his house (Matthew 12:29). Whether the binding is past or future is the core of the millennium debate.

A detail that matters for the debate: 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 all speak of gathering the nations for "the battle" (τὸν πόλεμον), and 19:17–21 and 20:8–9 both borrow from Ezekiel 38–39. Amillennial readers say these are one battle told three times. Premillennial readers say they are two battles, 1,000 years apart, and point to Isaiah 24:21–22, where hostile powers are locked in a dungeon, "and after many days they will be called to account."

Many early Christians expected the world to last 6,000 years, one "day" of a thousand years for each day of creation (Psalm 90:4), followed by a thousand-year Sabbath rest (Epistle of Barnabas 15). A similar idea appears in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 97a).

deep.title: Azi Dahaka, the dragon chained under a mountain
deep.note: very close story shape; written down much later (Pahlavi texts of the 800s AD)
deep.b: In Persian tradition the three-headed dragon Azi Dahaka is defeated by the hero Thraetaona (Fereydun in the later Shahnameh), who chains him inside Mount Damavand instead of killing him. Near the end of time he breaks free and ravages the world, until the hero Keresaspa rises and kills him. Bound, released for a short time, then destroyed: almost the exact shape of Revelation 20:1–10.

deep.title: Loki and the wolf Fenrir, bound until the end
deep.b: The gods bind the wolf Fenrir with a magic chain, and bind Loki in a cave, until Ragnarök. At the end they break loose, lead the giants and monsters against the gods, and fire consumes the world. Like Fimbulwinter, these stories were recorded by Christians around 1200, so the influence may run in either direction.

deep.title: Gog and Magog behind the wall
deep.b: The Qur'an tells of Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog), a destructive people shut behind a wall of iron and copper built by Dhul-Qarnayn. Near the end the wall gives way and they pour out over the earth (Surah 18:94–99; 21:96). Both traditions draw on Ezekiel 38–39.

"The camp of the saints and the beloved city" (20:9). The Greek joins the two with "and," so they may be one place or two. Premillennial readers see Jerusalem restored as Israel's capital. Amillennial readers see the church, which Hebrews 12:22 already calls "the heavenly Jerusalem."

echoes: Ezekiel 38–39; Daniel 7:9–10, 22; Isaiah 24:21–22; Matthew 12:29; Isaiah 65:17–25; Psalm 90:4

settings.what: The blessing on the first resurrection
settings.by: John
settings.to: the churches, and those who stay faithful to death
settings.when: after the vision of the martyrs who reign for a thousand years
settings.why: The fifth of the book's seven blessings tells hearers who feared death for their faith that the second death has no power over them, and that they will be "priests of God and of Christ." For a church that had lost Antipas, it is a promise that the faithful dead are not losers but rulers.
views: Premillennial readers, most futurists among them, expect a literal thousand-year reign after Christ returns.
Amillennial readers, following Augustine, read the thousand years as the church age now, with the martyrs reigning in heaven.
Some read it as a coming golden age of the gospel before Christ returns. Historicists have often held this or the amillennial view.

traditions.q: What are the thousand years (20:1–6), and when are they?
views: The present age of the church, in which Christ already reigns with his saints (Augustine). The Church rejects millenarianism, the hope of an earthly kingdom of Christ within history, even in milder forms (Catechism 676).
The time between Christ's first coming and the end, as Andrew of Caesarea taught. Some early fathers, such as Papias and Irenaeus, expected an earthly reign, but the church did not follow them.
The present reign of Christ. The Augsburg Confession (article 17) rejects the "Jewish opinions" that before the resurrection the godly will take over the kingdoms of the world.

No confession decides, and Reformed churches hold two views. Amillennialists (such as Anthony Hoekema) say it is the present church age; postmillennialists (many Puritans, Jonathan Edwards, B. B. Warfield) expect the gospel to win most of the world before Christ returns.

Divided. Baptists hold every view, and the Baptist Faith and Message (article 10) says only that God will bring the world to its end in his own time and way. Historic premillennialists like Ladd expect Christ to return before an earthly reign.

A literal future thousand years after Christ returns, when he reigns on earth from Jerusalem and God's promises to Israel as a nation are fulfilled. The Assemblies of God and many other Pentecostals hold a similar premillennial view.

Premillennial, but in heaven. At Christ's return the saved are taken to heaven for the thousand years while the earth lies empty and Satan is bound there with no one to tempt; then the holy city comes down, and the wicked are destroyed.

traditions.q: What is the lake of fire (20:10, 14–15): punishment without end, an end of existence, or a fire that may in the end restore?
views: Hell is real and eternal. Those who die unrepentant in mortal sin go to its "eternal fire," whose chief punishment is eternal separation from God; God predestines no one to it (Catechism 1033–1037). Some Catholic theologians, such as Hans Urs von Balthasar, argue that we may hope all will be saved, while holding that hell is a real possibility.

The punishment of the age to come does not end, and the teaching that all must be restored, linked with Origen, was condemned in the sixth century. Many Orthodox teachers add that the fire is God's love felt as torment by those who refuse it (Isaac the Syrian), and some, after Gregory of Nyssa, hope that all may yet be saved. Kallistos Ware puts it this way: to say all must be saved is heresy, but to hope that all may be saved is allowed.
Eternal punishment. The Augsburg Confession (article 17) condemns those who teach that the punishments of the damned and of the devils will come to an end.
Eternal punishment. The Westminster Confession (33.2) says the wicked will be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.

Not settled by the Thirty-Nine Articles. The Church of England's Doctrine Commission (The Mystery of Salvation, 1995) leaned toward final destruction rather than endless torment, and the evangelical Anglican John Stott tentatively held conditional immortality; many Anglicans hold the traditional view.

Mostly eternal punishment: the Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 10) says the unrighteous will be consigned to hell, the place of everlasting punishment, and the 1689 London Confession (32.2) agrees. Some Baptist and other evangelical scholars, such as Edward Fudge, hold conditional immortality.

Annihilation (conditional immortality). Only God is immortal by nature; at the end fire from God consumes the wicked, and sin and sinners are gone forever (Fundamental Beliefs 26–27). "Forever and ever" in 20:10 is read as a result that never ends, not as endless conscious pain.

title: The New Jerusalem
sum: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, "and the sea is no longer there." The holy city comes down out of heaven like a bride. "Look! God's tent is with human beings." He will wipe every tear; death, grief, crying and pain will be gone. "Look, I am making all things new."

The city's twelve gates carry the names of Israel's twelve tribes; its twelve foundations carry the names of the twelve apostles. It is 12,000 stadia (about 1,400 miles) long, wide and high, with gates of pearl and a street of gold. There is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates are never shut.

Then comes a hard verse. Right after the promise "I will be his God, and he will be my son," 21:8 lists the cowardly, the unfaithful, murderers, liars and others, and says their share is in "the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death." Below the four views are a closer look at what that verse does and does not say, what "the second death" meant to John's first readers, and a guide to the parts of the city.
