readings: Read literally
A real physical city, about 1,400 miles on each side and just as tall.
Read as symbol

If the city is a cube, the only other cube in the Bible is the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20). The whole city has become the Holy of Holies, where everyone lives in God's presence. The city is also the bride (21:9–10), so the city is the people.

views.P: The new-covenant people of God after the first things passed away in AD 70 (Hebrews 8:13), real now and complete in the future.
views.H: The final, eternal state after history ends.
views.F: The eternal state after the millennium.
views.I: The church's final destiny and its true identity even now.

deep.b:
Does 21:8 cancel forgiveness?

Read on its own, 21:8 can sound like "sinners burn in hell." Read in its setting, it says something narrower and more pointed. Five things in the text itself are worth noticing.

1. It describes people who stay that way, not people who once did those things. Paul gives a very similar list, then tells the Corinthians that some of them used to be these very things, "but you were washed" (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Revelation says the same thing in its own picture language. The people inside the city are not people who never sinned. They are people who "washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (7:14; 22:14). The difference between inside and outside is not a clean record but a washing.

2. Revelation keeps offering forgiveness up to its last page. Even "Jezebel" is given "time to repent" (2:21). Two verses before 21:8, God says, "To anyone who is thirsty I will give water from the spring of the water of life as a free gift" (21:6). The book's last invitation is "Let whoever wants it take the water of life as a free gift" (22:17). And the plagues keep noting, with sorrow, that people refused to repent (9:20–21; 16:9, 11). Repentance is open until it is refused.

3. The list starts with Christians who give up. "Cowardly" (deiloi) and "unfaithful" (apistoi, "faithless") come first, before murderers. In a book written to persecuted churches, the cowardly are believers who deny Jesus to save themselves, the opposite of Antipas, who "did not deny" (2:13), and of the martyrs who "did not love their lives" (12:11). The verse is the dark twin of 21:7: "The one who wins the victory will inherit these things." It is a warning aimed first at the church, not a verdict on everyone outside it.

4. "Liars" is a loyalty word. In Revelation the liars are false apostles (2:2), people who "say they are Jews and are not, but are lying" (3:9), and the false prophet. In the mouths of the 144,000 "not one lie was found" (14:5). Lying here means a false allegiance, the opposite of Jesus, "the faithful witness" (1:5).

5. "Their share" is an inheritance word. The Greek to meros autōn means "their portion," an inheritance word. Revelation uses the same word for those who have "a share in the first resurrection," over whom "the second death has no power" (20:6), and for a "share in the tree of life" (22:19). Everyone receives a share. The question the verse presses is which one you are choosing.

So 21:8 does not take back forgiveness. It assumes it: the cure for every item on the list is offered, free, in the verses on either side. What it denies is that someone can keep refusing the cure and still end up inside. The deeper questions are still debated (see "The second death," next), but none of the major Christian views reads this verse as "no forgiveness for murderers or liars."

Is this "hell"?

Not in the way the word is usually used. Modern translations of Revelation never use the word "hell." The KJV's "hell" (1:18; 6:8; 20:13–14) translates Hadēs, the realm of the dead, the grave. And in 20:14 Hades itself is thrown into the lake of fire. So "hell" and "the lake of fire" are not the same thing in Revelation; one is emptied into the other.

The New Testament has several different words that English Bibles often flatten into "hell": Hadēs (the grave, Sheol); Gehenna (the burning valley outside Jerusalem, Jesus's word, Mark 9:43–48); Tartarus (a prison for fallen angels, 2 Peter 2:4); and Revelation's own "lake of fire." Keeping them apart helps you hear what each passage actually says.

The second death

The phrase appears four times in the Bible, all in Revelation: 2:11; 20:6; 20:14; 21:8. It is defined twice: as the lake of fire (20:14), and as the lake that burns with fire and sulfur (21:8).

Where it came from. It was not John's invention. The Aramaic Targums, the paraphrases of Scripture read aloud in synagogues, use "the second death" for final judgment after the first, physical death. Targum Onkelos on Deuteronomy 33:6 reads, "Let Reuben live, and not die the second death." The Targum of Jeremiah 51:39 and 57 says Babylon's rulers will "die the second death and not live in the world to come." The Targum of Isaiah uses it as well (22:14; 65:6, 15). The Targums reached their written form after John's time, but they preserve older synagogue usage, and for John's Jewish readers the phrase likely already meant "shut out of the world to come." Notice that the Jeremiah Targum uses it of Babylon, the same enemy Revelation has just watched fall.

A comfort before it is a threat. Its first use is a promise to Smyrna, a church about to suffer and die: "The one who wins the victory will never be harmed by the second death" (2:11). The point is that the first death, the one Rome can inflict, is not the one that matters. Jesus said, "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).

A pair with the first resurrection. "Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power" (20:6). Augustine explained the pairing this way: there is a first resurrection of the soul now (coming to life in Christ, John 5:24–25) and a second of the body later; a first death of the body and a second, final death. An old Christian saying puts it: "Born once, die twice. Born twice, die once."

What it means: the three main views.

  • Eternal conscious punishment. The second death is unending separation from God, felt forever. This is the historic majority view (Augustine, Aquinas, most Reformers), citing 14:11 and 20:10.
  • Conditional immortality (annihilationism). "Death" means what it says: the end of existence, final and permanent. Only God has immortality by nature (1 Timothy 6:16). Held by John Stott (cautiously) and Edward Fudge, and growing among evangelicals.
  • Hopeful universalism. The fire purifies, and in the end all may be restored, pointing to the open gates and the healing of the nations (21:25; 22:2). Held by Origen and some modern writers; a minority view that must explain 22:15, where some are still "outside."

A Greek parallel: Plutarch (about AD 100) also wrote of a "second death," the soul's final separation from the mind after the first death (On the Face of the Moon 943). It is a different idea with no known link to Revelation.

deep.title: The second death is what happens to death
deep.b: The book shows Death as a rider (6:8) and Death and Hades as a pair that hold the dead (1:18; 20:13). In 20:14 they are thrown into the lake, and only then does John say "this is the second death." My reading: the first thing that "dies the second death" is death itself. That is why the very next scene can say "Death will be gone" (21:4). The people of 21:8 are those who keep holding on to what is being destroyed. They tie their lives to the losing side, the way the kings tie themselves to Babylon and then mourn her (18:9). This is not a new doctrine, and it does not settle the debate between the views above. It is a way of seeing that the lake is first of all God ending everything that ruins his world, and that the warning of 21:8 is "don't be found holding on to it."

Is the city literal or symbolic?

Literal readers (for example, John Walvoord and many dispensational teachers) take the city as a real place of real size, about 1,400 miles on each side, where the redeemed will live. Most other readers think it is a real future described in symbols, and the text gives several clues pointing that way:

  • The angel says one thing and shows another. "I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb," he says, and then he shows John a city (21:9–10). Earlier, the prostitute "is the great city" (17:18). Both women are cities and both cities are peoples. The new Jerusalem is first of all God's people.
  • The numbers do not fit together as architecture. The city is 12,000 stadia high, but its wall is 144 cubits (about 216 feet), tiny against a 1,400-mile height. Both numbers are built on twelve. They make sense as meaning, not as blueprints.
  • The materials are impossible on purpose. Gold "like glass you can see through" (21:21) is not a metal anyone has seen. Each gate is one pearl.
  • "By human measure, which is the angel's measure" (21:17). This seems to say that the angel's numbers are given in our units so that we can read their meaning.

A middle position is common: the new creation is a real, bodily, physical future (Romans 8:21; 1 Corinthians 15), and the city is a picture of what it will be like and who will be there.

The parts of the city, and what they may mean

Coming down from heaven (21:2, 10)

Ancient cities claimed to be founded by gods or heroes. Babel's builders wanted "a city, and a tower with its head in the heavens" (Genesis 11:4). This city is not built up by people; it comes down from God, as a gift.

A bride (21:2, 9)

The city is a people. Compare Babylon, a prostitute dressed in gold, jewels and pearls (17:4). The bride is built from the same materials, but they are her structure, not her costume.

A high mountain (21:10)

Ezekiel was taken "to a very high mountain" to see the new temple city (Ezekiel 40:2), and Isaiah saw the LORD's mountain raised above all others (Isaiah 2:2). John saw Babylon from a wilderness (17:3); he sees the bride from a mountain.

Like jasper (21:11, 18)

The one on the throne "looked like jasper stone" (4:3). The city shines with God's own appearance.

A great, high wall (21:12, 17)

Walls meant safety and identity: you were either a citizen or not. With gates that never close (21:25), this wall is not for defense. It marks who belongs.

Twelve gates, three on each side, with tribal names (21:12–13)

Israel camped around the tabernacle three tribes to a side (Numbers 2). Ezekiel's city has twelve gates named for the tribes, three on each side (Ezekiel 48:30–35), and its name is "The LORD is there." An Aramaic text from the Dead Sea Scrolls, the "Description of the New Jerusalem" (4Q554 and others), also imagines a vast, measured city with twelve gates named for the tribes. John was writing within a known Jewish hope.

Twelve foundations with the apostles' names (21:14)

"Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20). Israel on the gates, apostles underneath: one city for the people of both covenants.

The gold measuring rod (21:15)

In Ezekiel 40:3 and Zechariah 2:1–5, measuring means God claims and protects a place. John measured the temple in 11:1 while the outer court was trampled; now the whole city is measured and nothing is left out.

As tall as it is wide (21:16)

The city's length, width and height are equal. Most readers picture a cube (some, a pyramid). The only cube in Scripture is the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple, 20 cubits each way, overlaid with pure gold (1 Kings 6:20). Only the high priest entered it, once a year. Now the whole city is that room, and everyone lives there.

Pure gold, clear as glass (21:18, 21)

The Most Holy Place was lined with gold (1 Kings 6:20–22). The city is made of what used to line God's private room. Glass in the Roman world was a luxury, and clear glass was hard to make; the image is of perfect purity with nothing hidden.

Twelve foundation jewels (21:19–20)

They echo the twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate, each engraved with a tribe's name (Exodus 28:17–21), and Isaiah's promise of a city rebuilt with sapphires and rubies (Isaiah 54:11–12). The people once carried over the high priest's heart are now the city's foundation.

Gates of single pearls (21:21)

Pearls were the most prized gems in Rome; Pliny says they held "the highest rank among all valuables" (Natural History 9.106). A later rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 75a) says God will set huge single gems, 30 cubits across, as the gates of Jerusalem. In Jesus's parable the kingdom is like a merchant who found "one pearl worth a great deal" (Matthew 13:45–46).

One main street of gold (21:21; 22:1–2)

Greek and Roman cities in Asia were built around a grand colonnaded main street. Ephesus had its marble harbor street, later rebuilt by the emperor Arcadius (about AD 400) as the Arcadian Way and lit at night. This city's main street is gold, and down its middle runs the river of life (22:1–2).

No temple, no sun, no night (21:22–25)

Every city in Asia was proud of its temples: Artemis at Ephesus, Zeus at Pergamum, the emperor in nearly all seven. This city has none, "because the Lord God, the Almighty, is its temple, and so is the Lamb." "No longer will the sun be your light by day... The LORD will be your light forever" (Isaiah 60:19–20).

Gates never shut (21:25–26)

Ancient city gates were closed every night against raiders, and opened by day for trade. Isaiah 60:11: "Your gates will stand open all the time; day and night they will not be shut, so that the wealth of nations can be brought to you." No enemies are left, so there is nothing to shut out.

Nothing unclean enters (21:27)

From Isaiah 52:1. Who gets in is decided by one thing: "those who are written in the Lamb's book of life." The entry list is the Lamb's, which is the answer to the worry about 21:8.

deep.title: A Babylon that has been turned inside out
deep.b: The Greek historian Herodotus, read by educated people all over Asia Minor, described ancient Babylon as a perfect square, 120 stadia on each side, with a huge wall, a hundred bronze gates, and the Euphrates running through the middle of the city (Histories 1.178–180). John's city is also a square, with a wall, many gates, and a river running down its middle (22:1). My suggestion: John's first readers would have heard the new Jerusalem as the true version of the famous great city. Babylon's river was a highway for trade and an invasion route (Cyrus took the city by diverting it); this city's river is the water of life. Babylon's gates kept enemies out; this city's gates never close. Babylon's merchants grew rich from its wealth (18:11–19); here the kings bring their glory in as a gift (21:24–26). Many scholars contrast the two cities as the two women of chapters 17 and 21. The link to Herodotus's square, walled, river city is my own, and I have not found it argued in the commentaries I know.

deep.title: Frashokereti, the world made wonderful
deep.b: Zoroastrian teaching ends history with the "making wonderful": the dead are raised, everyone passes through a river of molten metal that feels like warm milk to the good and burns the wicked, evil is destroyed, and the world is made new and perfect forever. The parallel to resurrection, judgment and a new creation is clear. How much Persian thought shaped Jewish and Christian hope is still argued.

deep.title: The green world after Ragnarök
deep.b: After the fire, the Norse earth rises again out of the sea, green and fair. Fields grow without being sown, and the surviving gods find their golden game pieces lying in the grass (Völuspá 59–62). Revelation's new world is similar in its renewal and different in one telling detail: there is no sea at all.

Twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles. Neither group replaces the other. Both are built into one city, and you enter through Israel's names and stand on the apostles'.

deep.title: "No more sea": the barrier is gone
deep.b: The sea is where the beast came from (13:1), so its end means the end of chaos and evil. That reading is common. I would add a temple layer. Before God's throne there was "a sea of glass" (4:6; 15:2). Solomon's temple also had a huge bronze basin called "the Sea," where priests washed before they could serve (1 Kings 7:23; 2 Chronicles 4:6). In Revelation 4 the sea of glass stands between the throne and everyone else. In the new creation there is no sea and no temple, and the people see God's face. My speculation: "no more sea" also means no more barrier and no more need to be washed before you may come close. The washing has already happened ("they washed their robes," 7:14; 22:14).

deep.title: The angel at Eden’s gate becomes twelve angels at open gates
deep.b: After the fall, God placed cherubim at the east of Eden with a flaming sword "to guard the way to the tree of life" (Genesis 3:24). In the New Jerusalem there are angels at the gates again, twelve of them (21:12), but the gates are never shut (21:25), and the tree of life is inside. Revelation 22:14 then blesses those who "may go in through the gates" to "the tree of life." My speculation: the angels at the gates are the cherub of Genesis 3 turned around, no longer guarding the way to the tree but standing beside open doors. Commentators often note the return of the tree of life. Pairing Eden's guard with the city's twelve gatekeepers is my own connection.

echoes: Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 25:8; Ezekiel 40–48; Isaiah 60:11, 19; 1 Kings 6:20; Exodus 28:17–21; Leviticus 26:11–12

settings.what: The voice from the throne
settings.by: a loud voice from the throne, then God himself
settings.to: John and the churches, and "the one who is thirsty"
settings.when: as the new Jerusalem comes down out of heaven
settings.why: God promises to live with his people, wipe every tear and end death and pain. He offers the water of life as a free gift, and names "the one who wins the victory" as his heir, the same promise made at the end of each of the seven letters. The warning list that follows (the cowardly, the idol worshipers, the liars) reminds the churches that the choices in chapters 2–3 decide who enters.

title: The River, the Tree, and "Come"
sum: The river of the water of life flows from God's throne down the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, its leaves for the healing of the nations. There is no more curse. "They will see his face."

Then the book closes. Jesus says "I am coming soon" three times. John is told not to seal the book, "because the time is near." The Spirit and the bride say, "Come!" A warning follows not to add or take away. The last words are a promise and a prayer: "Yes, I am coming soon." "Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!"

readings: Read literally
Christ could return at any moment. "Soon" is measured by God's clock (2 Peter 3:8).
Read as symbol
Genesis began with a garden, a river and a tree, and lost them. Revelation ends with all three restored inside a city. The book ends as it began, as a letter to be read aloud in church.

views.P: "Near" meant near for the first readers, and much of the book came true in AD 70.
views.H: The whole of history from John's day to ours fits inside the book.
views.F: The return is imminent, and the warnings are for the last generation.
views.I: Every generation lives "near" the end and should live ready.

deep.b:
How the book’s ending answers its beginning

Chapter 1Chapter 22
God sends his angel to show his slaves what must happen soon (1:1)The same words: "to show his slaves what must soon take place" (22:6)
A blessing on those who hear and keep what is written (1:3)"Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy" (22:7)
"I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God (1:8)"I am the Alpha and the Omega," says Jesus (22:13)
"I, John" (1:9)"I, John" (22:8)
John is told to write and send the book to the seven churches (1:11)The angel sent to bear witness "for the churches" (22:16)
He is coming with the clouds (1:7)"Yes, I am coming soon" (22:20)
A greeting of grace and peace (1:4)"The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all" (22:21)

The book is framed like a letter, with a greeting and a farewell. The title God gives himself at the start, Jesus claims at the end.

Do not add or take away

22:18–19 warns against adding to or taking from "the words of this book." Moses gave the same warning for the law (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Ancient authors sometimes added such curses to protect their books from careless copyists; Irenaeus ended one of his works by asking copyists to check their copy carefully against the original (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 5.20.2). The warning is about this book, not the whole Bible, which did not yet exist as one volume.

"Come, Lord Jesus"

The book's last prayer (22:20) is the Greek form of an Aramaic prayer from the earliest church, Maranatha, "Our Lord, come!" Paul quotes it untranslated (1 Corinthians 16:22), and the Didache uses it in its prayers after the Lord's Supper (Didache 10.6). It may have been said at the meal. Revelation ends where Christian worship began: asking Jesus to come.

echoes: Genesis 2:9–10; Genesis 3:22–24; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Zechariah 14:8, 11; Daniel 12:4; Isaiah 11:1; Numbers 24:17; Deuteronomy 4:2

settings.what: The closing words
settings.by: the angel, Jesus, the Spirit and the bride, and John
settings.to: the seven churches who hear the book read aloud, and everyone who hears it
settings.when: at the end of the book, as the letter closes
settings.why: The ending returns to the churches and to the urgency of the start: "Look, I am coming soon!" John is told not to seal the book, "because the time is near": it was meant for its first hearers, not to be locked away for a far future. Jesus speaks in his own name: "I, Jesus, sent my angel to bear witness to you about these things for the churches." The invitation to come and drink, the warning not to add to or take from the book, and the prayer "Come, Lord Jesus!" end it as worship, as it would have been heard in the gathering.
views: Preterists read "soon" and "near" as pointing to events in the first readers' lifetime. Historicists read them as the start of a sequence that began in John's day and runs through church history. Futurists read them as the certainty or suddenness of Christ's return. Idealists read them as the nearness of judgment and hope in every age.
